US-backed consortium proposes $4.4bn LNG project. • Proposal envisages four tanks holding 560,000 cubic metres at Port Qasim in first phase of the $4.4bn plan that also includes a 1,100km upcountry gas pipeline • Project would charge $4.93 per mmBtu for terminal and storage, $1.91 for transmission over first decade ISLAMABAD: A private consortium of US companies, backed by the Trump administration, is pushing for an investment of up to $4.4 billion in an integrated liquefied natural gas (LNG) project in Pakistan, covering imports, storage, re-gasification, gas transmission and sales to large consumers on a ‘merchant basis’. The development comes after Energas, an earlier frontrunner consisting of the Lucky Group and QatarEnergy, abandoned a similar project citing fundamental changes in Pakistan’s energy policy and requirements, as well as longstanding unresolved policy and fiscal issues. The US consortium comprises Global Vision Energy Partners (GVEP) and Khanjee Holdings, both related firms, along with strategic co-investors from other countries and General Mediterranean Holding, a Luxem­bo­urg-based US financial conglomerate. The sponsors have reportedly sec­ured consent from the Port Qasim Aut­hority for the proposed project site. An application has also been filed with the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) for a provisional licence. A special purpose vehicle (SPV), a separate legal entity established to hold specific assets and liabilities and isolate financial risks, has been incorporated. Government facilitation has also been conveyed through the Mini­stry of Maritime Affairs and the Mini­stry of Energy’s Petroleum Divi­sion, according to documents seen by Dawn. The project has been approved for consideration under the US Trade and Development Agency’s (USTDA) project preparation programme. It may also receive partial financing from the US Development Finance Corporation, backed by export credit guarantees from the US Export-Import Bank for technology, equipment and services. Pakistan currently has no LNG storage facilities, leaving its domestic re-gasified LNG supplies entirely dependent on import supply chains and international energy prices. The sponsors plan to develop the project in two phases. The first phase will comprise an LNG terminal and storage facility with four tanks and an estimated annual throughput of 35 billion cubic feet (BCF), at a cost of $1.7bn. The second phase will involve the construction of a 1,100km, 42-48-inch pipeline to transport gas upcountry, with a capacity of around 1.2 billion cubic feet per day (BCFD). This will take the total project cost to $4.4bn. The government had previously pursued a similar North-South gas pipeline project with Russia. The proposed venture is being structured as a merchant infrastructure platform to meet domestic regasification requirements while establishing a physical LNG storage and trading hub in South Asia for US and Middle Eastern suppliers. The consortium is engaging local inve­stors for up to 10 per cent equity participation, with indicative investments starting at $50 million per investor. The sponsors also expect to attract strategic co-investors, including global energy and infrastructure funds and institutional investors such as Grey Rock Investment Partners, Kohlberg Kravis Roberts & Co, Blackstone Inc., Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund and the Kuwait Investment Authority. Their participation remains subject to due diligence, investment approvals and definitive agreements. No binding equity commitments have been confirmed so far. The SPV will develop, own and operate the project as a regional LNG storage, regasification and trading hub, serving Pakistan’s domestic gas market alongside US and Middle Eastern LNG suppliers. The model will not depend on a single government-backed offtake arrangement. Re-gasification tariffs for the domestic market will be submitted to Ogra for approval, while other commercial services, including storage, tolling and transshipment, will be priced on market-based terms. The US sponsors consider Port Qasim strategically important because of its existing port infrastructure and marine access for LNG carriers. Its location outside the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most significant energy shipping chokepoints, is another key consideration. Under the proposed financing structure, the project will have a 70:30 debt-to-equity ratio. GVEP will hold a 26pc stake, followed by General Mediterranean Holding with 24pc, and Khanjee Holdings and strategic co-investors with 20pc each. Local investors will hold the remaining 10pc in the first phase, which is estimated to cost $1.32bn (70pc of the $1.7bn cost). The final project cost will be determined after the execution of engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) contracts and other construction and supply agreements. The commercial model is expected to combine long-term tolling and storage agreements, transshipment arrangements and take-or-pay commitments where appropriate, with the remaining capacity reserved for merchant activities. The proposed tolling tariff for the terminal and storage facility is $4.93 per million British thermal units (mmBtu), while the separate transmission tariff is estimated at $1.91 per mmBtu for the first 10 years. These rates are projected to decline to $2.20 and $0.92 per mmBtu, respectively, thereafter. The LNG terminal and storage facility will have four tanks, each with a capacity of 140,000 cubic metres, providing total static storage capacity of 560,000 cubic metres. Based on three inventory turnover cycles annually, the facility is expected to handle approximately 35.6BCF of LNG a year, with storage capacity of around 11.9BCF per cycle. Kabul warned of ‘unbearable punishment’ as clashes persist along border. • Torkham stays shut for five hours following firefight over disputed check post • Military spox says Afghan Taliban ‘won’t be able to bear cost’ of harbouring terrorists • Names India as ‘prime contractor’ behind terrorism in Pakistan • Rubio says US shares Pakistan’s concerns over attacks from Afghan soil, open to role in easing tensions KHYBER/LOWER SOUTH WAZIRISTAN: Pakistani and Afghan border forces exchanged fire at several points along their border on Sunday, as the military warned that the Afghan Taliban would not be able to withstand the “punishment” Islamabad could inflict if Kabul failed to rein in terrorists. The fresh clashes temporarily shut down the busy Torkham border crossing over a disputed check post and killed one civilian in mortar shelling near the Angoor Adda crossing. The situation unfolded as Washington validated Pakistan’s concerns regarding cross-border terrorist attacks originating from Afghanistan and signalled openness to playing a productive role in easing tensions. The situation at the Torkham cro­ssing stabilised after a nearly five-hour closure caused by an hou­rlong exchange of light-arms fire. It reopened only after border officials from both countries agreed through intermediaries to halt all construction near the border. However, tensions remained high in the Angoor Adda area of Lower South Waziristan. According to the deputy commissioner of Lower South Wazir­istan, Taliban fighters continued to target Pakistani border checkpoints with unprovoked firing. Pakistani security forces responded immediately and effectively, targeting “multiple Afghan border posts, mortar positions, and defensive checkpoints”, the official wrote on X, adding that no reports of any casualties have emerged from the border areas on the Pakistani side. Border clashes According to locals, gunfire erupted at Torkham on Sunday when Afghan authorities once again started construction on a disputed check post. Authorities at Torkham said the Afghan side began work on the controversial Zangali check post, situated within a 100-metre radius of the Afghan side of the border, despite Pakistan’s strong objections. The firing continued for nearly an hour with no casualties on the Pakistani side. The two nations had previously agreed to refrain from building security structures within a 100-metre radius of the border. The intense firing caused the immediate closure of the border and panic among returning Afghans and local residents. During the standoff, resident Siraj Khan told Dawn that he saw about 20 vehicles carrying unregistered Afghan families hastily returning from the border at Zero Point amid the crossfire. The repatriation of unregistered Afghans was suspended, and government offices were closed. Meanwhile, tensions escalated in the Angoor Adda area after two mortar shells were reportedly fired from the Afghan side. Military’s warning The flare-ups underscored a stark warning delivered by Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) chief, Lt Gen Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry. In an interview with a news agency earlier this week, portions of which were broadcast by state media on Sunday, the military’s spokesperson said Pakistan has the operational readiness and a clear strategy to impose a heavy cost on the interim Afghan leadership if terrorism continues originating from Afghan soil. “Whatever they want to send, they can, they may try. We have the capability to take them out,” Lt Gen Chaudhry said. “They don’t have, I think, the capability to then absorb the punishment that we can [inflict].” He noted that Pakistan has no desire to interfere in Afghanistan’s internal governance. “We only ask that you don’t support terrorism inside Pakistan. Stop harbouring the terrorist leaders,” he added. The ISPR chief asserted that while foreign military forces have physically withdrawn from Afghanistan, the Afghan Taliban front continues to operate as a proxy for multiple external parties, singling out India as the primary sponsor of anti-Pakistan terrorism. “In the case of Pakistan, the prime contractor is India, and the proxies are TTP and the BLA,” he said, describing New Delhi as “the biggest terror sponsor here” and stating that “as far as terrorism in Pakistan is concerned, they [the Afghan Taliban] are a proxy of the Indians”. Addressing whether Pakistan fears a cross-border drone dynamic similar to Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia, Lt Gen Chaudhry noted Afghanistan has no domestic drone industry and relies entirely on external sponsors. “The capability of Afghans, whatever they have, firstly it’s not their own. There’s no drone industry, there is no technology of that sort in Afghanistan. So it’s been provided by the sponsors, the terror sponsors, because the biggest terror sponsor here is India,” he said. The ISPR chief emphasised that the Pakistan Army is systematically adapting to the changing character of modern warfare across contact and non-contact domains, cyber operations, drones and long-range munitions. US shares Pakistan’s concerns The security concerns were echoed in Washington’s diplomatic messaging, as Secretary of State Marco Rubio affirmed that the US shares Pakistan’s concerns regarding cross-border terrorist attacks originating from Afghanistan and signalled openness to playing a productive role in easing tensions. “We don’t want Pakistan to be targeted for terrorism,” he told reporters at the G20 foreign ministers meeting in Atlanta, Georgia. “Pakistan is concerned about terrorist attacks that are being sponsored from the territory of Afghanistan. They think that the Taliban has not done enough to constrain those attacks,” Mr Rubio said, noting that Pakistan had taken action in response to the threat. He added that Washington did not have close relations with the Taliban authorities in Afghanistan and the US opposed terrorism regardless of where it originated or whom it targeted. “We’ve heard the concerns that Pakistan has raised, and we’ve seen some of those attacks that they point to,” Rubio said. “We’re against terrorism no matter where it emanates from and who it targets.” With input from APP Published in Dawn, November 2nd, 2026

Reko Diq project may face further delay. Production at the Reko Diq copper-gold project could be delayed by two years to 2030, pending improved security in Balochistan and de-escalation in the Middle East crisis, according to government sources and industry insiders. War in the neighbouring Iran alongside persistent security challenges in Balochistan have reportedly pushed investors to adjust the original 2028 timeline. Canadian mining titan Barrick Mining (formerly Gold) Corporation is expected to resume full-scale development by mid-2027 following an ongoing internal project review. While the company has yet to issue an official announcement, its local officials express optimism that the multibillion-dollar venture remains on track. Despite the operational slowdown, the project management has retained all 700 permanent and roughly 2,000 contractual workers at the site, though some third-party service contracts were allowed to expire. Barrick, as well as senior federal and Balochistan provincial government officials, did not immediately respond to requests for their comment. Iran situation alongside persistent security challenges in Balochistan has reportedly pushed investors to adjust the 2028 timeline Despite recent timeline concerns, the company sources maintain that daily operations on the ground remain active. “Research, administrative work, and community development projects are progressing normally,” said a company employee speaking on condition of anonymity. “Speculation about the project’s future is baseless and fuelled by ill-informed or irresponsible elements.” Another official echoed this confidence, pointing out that nearly $1 billion has already been invested in the venture. “The project is technically viable and holds immense promise for all stakeholders. External factors may delay it, but the stakes are too high for any shareholder — whether the miner or the government — to walk away now.” Adding momentum to upcoming industry talks, Barrick Mining Chairman John L. Thornton is expected to visit Pakistan later this month to attend the Pakistan Minerals Investment Forum 2026 in Islamabad. However, industry experts remain divided over the financial fallout of potential delays. A private-sector source involved in another Balochistan mining venture warned of severe cost overruns, advocating for a consortium of local companies to acquire a minority stake. “Even if work resumes within a year, project costs could rise by $8bn to $10bn. Further security deterioration or delays exceeding two years could render it prohibitively expensive,” he cautioned. Conversely, an industry insider with business ties to the Reko Diq Mining Company (RDMC) dismissed the $10bn cost escalation estimate as “bordering on absurdity.” “Delays might raise costs by 10 per cent at most — roughly $450 million to $900m,” he estimated, adding that sentiment surrounding the project had improved sharply in recent weeks. “A month ago, I would have been uncertain. Today, I am confident that work on Reko Diq will resume sooner than expected.” He also expressed regret that the operator reportedly plans to process only 30pc to 35pc of the copper-gold output in Pakistan — potentially routing the remainder to its Australian facility — rather than maximising domestic value addition. In February this year, Barrick Mining initiated a formal review of Reko Diq, announcing a slowdown in development and extending its assessment period through early 2027. Speaking at the Mining Forum Americas last month, the Barrick CEO offered no revised construction timelines, noting: “We are revisiting it because we need some sort of security improvement before we would embark on a full construction schedule.” Canada’s Barrick Mining holds a 50pc stake in the project, with the remaining half split equally between the Balochistan provincial government and three Pakistani state-owned entities: Pakistan Petroleum, Oil and Gas Development Company, and Government Holdings Private. As one of Pakistan’s most ambitious infrastructure endeavours, Reko Diq’s estimated Phase 1 investment has escalated from $4bn to $5.6bn. Phase 2 is projected to require another $3.5bn, pushing total capital expenditure to roughly $9.1bn, up from earlier estimates of around $7bn. Designed as a conventional open-pit mining and processing operation, the site will yield high-grade copper-gold concentrate. Initial capacity is set at 45m tonnes of ore annually, which is expected to double to 90m tonnes upon Phase 2 completion. While the mine was originally slated for a 40-year operational lifecycle, an updated feasibility study revised that figure to 37 years to account for higher throughput. However, ongoing exploration and resource development could potentially extend the mine’s lifespan up to 80 years. Beyond its export and revenue potential, Reko Diq is expected to generate 7,500 jobs during peak construction and sustain around 4,000 permanent positions once operational. Based on long-term commodity price assumptions, projected free cash flow over 37 years is estimated at $74bn. Published in Dawn, The Business and Finance Weekly, November 2nd, 2026

PIA engineer gunned down in suspected targeted attack in Karachi's Gulistan-i-Jauhar. KARACHI: An engineer working with the Pakistan International Airlines (PIA) was shot dead in a suspected targeted attack in Gulistan-i-Jauhar on Sunday afternoon, police and rescue services officials said. Sharea Faisal SHO Anser Ahmed Butt said that Imtiaz Ahmed, 54, left his home in Block-13 to purchase bread when unidentified assailants riding a motorcycle targeted him and rode away. He said three bullets hit a nearby parked car while one bullet hit him that proved fatal. He was shifted to a nearby private hospital where doctors pronounced him dead on arrival. Later, the body was shifted to the Jinnah Postgraduate Medical Centre for a post-mortem examination. The SHO ruled out robbery, saying the exact motive would be ascertained after investigation. He said the deceased was originally from Lahore and that police had contacted his brother, who was on his way to Karachi. Formal proceedings to ascertain the motive and identify the killers would be initiated after his arrival, he added. He said the deceased’s wife was currently in Germany to visit their daughter. Governor Kundi says Centre failing to give KP support it deserves. PESHAWAR: Governor Faisal Karim Kundi has said that the federal government is failing to provide Khyber Pakhtunkhwa the support it deserves. Addressing the annual conference of Pakistan Association of Urological Surgeons here on Sunday, he said that ignoring KP must be brought to an end without further delay. He said that practical steps were required to improve the province’s health sector on the pattern of Punjab and Sindh. He said that medical conferences provided an important platform for promotion of knowledge, research, exchange of experiences and awareness about modern treatment methods, according to a statement. The governor stressed the need for ensuring quality and specialised healthcare services in merged districts, southern districts and far-flung areas of the province. He said that modern treatment facilities should not remain limited to big cities and every citizen must have equal access to healthcare. Says collective efforts needed to restore province’s positive image He stated that improvement of health infrastructure, provision of modern medical equipment, doctors’ training and promotion of medical research were essential for strengthening healthcare system. The governor said that professional organisations like Pakistan Association of Urological Surgeons could play a vital role in enhancing doctors’ capacity, training young medical experts and developing collaboration with public sector hospitals. He said the Rs70,000 monthly salary of house officers was insufficient and it would be reviewed. Meanwhile, during his address at Darbar-i-Aalia Murshadabad Sharif in the provincial capital, the governor said that lasting peace was essential for the province’s progress and prosperity. He stressed the need for collective contribution of all segments of the society for promoting positive image of the province. Mr Kundi said that religious scholars had a vital role to play in promoting peace, unity and harmony across the province. He added that ulema should use their influence to spread the message of tolerance, discourage extremism and support collective efforts for lasting peace in the province. In a statement issued from his office, the governor emphasised the need for unity, lasting peace, development, promotion of sports, effective utilisation of the province’s natural resources and collective efforts to ensure welfare and prosperity of the people. The ceremony was attended by former prime minister Shahid Khaqan Abbasi, governor’s adviser Tayab Qureshi and others, read an official statement. Mr Kundi said that the province had endured decades of terrorism and rendered immense sacrifices, with religious scholars, security personnel, politicians and innocent students, including the martyrs of Army Public School, laying down their lives for peace. He said that peace was the basic requirement for development. He said that the province was known for its resilience in the face of terrorism and was now determined to move towards lasting stability and progress. He said that KP had produced outstanding sportspersons from Mardan, Dera Ismail Khan and Bannu who had won international recognition. He said that youth should be provided with opportunities to excel in sports and other fields. He stated that the province was blessed with abundant natural resources including oil, gas, water resources, tourism potential and the Tarbela Dam, which could transform its economy if properly utilised. Recalling Peshawar’s past reputation as the ‘city of flowers’, the governor said that collective efforts were required to restore the province’s positive image. “Safety of our people comes first, followed by the development of the province and the progress of the country,” he said, adding that the province would witness significant positive change in the near future. He congratulated the newly-graduated Huffaz, distributed certificates among them, visited the institution’s library and appreciated its services in the field of education. Nine people dead in Learjet crash in south Florida, officials say. A Learjet crashed on Sunday afternoon in a residential area in Palm Beach County, Florida, ‌killing all nine people on board, US transportation officials said. The private jet had taken off from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was headed to North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said in a statement. Videos on social ​media showed the jet slamming into the ground next to a road and exploding. “It was a ​big-time tragedy that happened,” Florida Governor Ron DeSantis said at a press conference near ⁠the crash site in Lake Worth Beach. “When you see that video, it’s a jarring thing. It was like ​a missile coming down, and a massive explosion, debris going everywhere.” The National Transportation Safety Board said it had ​launched an investigation into the crash, which Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy called a “horrific tragedy”. FAA records list the Bombardier-made Learjet 60’s owner as a Delaware corporation. Canada-based Bombardier said it would fully support the investigation and cooperate as needed. The crash left a “massive crater” ​by the road near the entrance to a mobile home park, Palm Beach County Commissioner Joel Flores ​said at the news conference. About 600 people were being evacuated from the area and relocated to two shelters in the ‌county, ⁠Flores said. Heavy rainfall and thunderstorms were occurring in the area at the time, forecaster AccuWeather said in a statement. An audio recording from a Miami air traffic control centre posted on LiveATC , a site that broadcasts air traffic control communications, captured the plane’s final moments before the crash in unusual detail. At first, someone in the plane’s ​cockpit reported to an ​air traffic controller that ⁠they were “managing the ice” but faced “moderate” turbulence and were seeking “better rides”. Less than a minute later, the person said “Mayday, mayday”, reporting that the plane was suddenly descending at a ​rate of 10,000 feet per minute. Seconds later, the person said they were declaring ​an emergency, ⁠with the rate of descent accelerating to 20,000 feet per minute. Less than 20 seconds later, the person said: “We’re going to crash into the ground” before saying that the descent rate had reached 22,000 feet per minute as the ⁠plane started ​banking. About 35 seconds after the initial mayday announcement, the last thing ​heard from the cockpit was a rapidly spoken “We’re out of time”. Flight tracking website Flightradar24 said data showed the vertical descent rate at ​one point exceeded 32,000 feet per minute.

Lahore's air quality index crosses 530 as pollution reaches hazardous levels. LAHORE: Air pollution in Lahore reached hazardous levels on Monday, with the Air Quality Index (AQI) crossing 530 and fine particulate matter (PM2.5) concentrations climbing to 343 micrograms per cubic metre. Several other cities in Punjab also recorded extremely high pollution levels, according to air quality monitoring platform IQAir. At 8am, IQAir recorded an AQI of 535 in Lahore, placing the city in the hazardous category. PM2.5 concentration, referring to tiny particles that can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream, stood at 343µg/m³. Air quality had already deteriorated sharply in the early morning, with hourly readings also entering the hazardous range. Figure shows the top ranked polluted cities according to IQAir on Friday morning. — Screengrab via IQAir The deterioration was not confined to the provincial capital. IQAir’s live ranking of Pakistani cities on Monday morning placed five Punjab cities among the country’s six most polluted urban centres. Gujranwala topped the ranking with an AQI of 606, followed by Lahore at 509, Faisalabad and Multan at 310 each, and Sialkot at 260. Peshawar ranked sixth with an AQI of 216. The readings varied across monitoring updates, with Gujranwala subsequently recording 675 and Lahore 535 in separate hourly updates, highlighting the rapidly changing pollution situation. Figure shows the top ranked polluted cities in Pakistan according to IQAir on Friday morning. — Screengrab via IQAir The worsening air quality comes amid a sharp increase in agricultural fire detections across Punjab. According to an analysis published by environmental monitoring website HamariHawa, Nasa satellites detected 13,241 fire spots in Pakistani Punjab between Oct 1 and 29, compared with 3,158 in Indian Punjab — 4.2 times as many. Around 92 per cent of the detected fires in Pakistani Punjab were located on farmland and were likely associated with crop-residue burning. The analysis found that 6,655 fire spots, around half of the monthly total, were detected during the last seven days of October. Oct 29 recorded the highest number of detections, at 1,327. Okara recorded the highest number of fire spots at 2,144, followed by Gujranwala with 1,011 and Nankana Sahib with 1,003. The findings point to extensive agricultural burning in the rice-growing belt surrounding Lahore. Smoke from these fires, along with emissions from vehicles, industries and other sources, adds to the regional pollution burden. Weather conditions, including weak winds and atmospheric inversions, can further trap pollutants close to the ground. Weather factor Meanwhile, a new analysis by the Pakistan Air Quality Initiative (PAQI) has questioned the extent of improvement in Lahore’s air quality during October, despite government claims that the city experienced its cleanest October in five years. According to PAQI, average PM2.5 concentrations in October 2026 fell by 27 per cent compared with the same month last year across 26 monitoring sites. However, after accounting for weather conditions, the improvement was estimated at just four per cent. The analysis attributed a substantial part of the decline to weather conditions, particularly a deeper nighttime atmospheric mixing layer, which allowed pollutants more room to disperse. The remaining improvement reflected the combined effects of government measures, changes in agricultural burning and other pollution sources. However, the analysis could not establish the individual contribution of each factor. Despite the decline, PM2.5 concentrations exceeded Pakistan’s prescribed daily limit on every day in October, according to PAQI. The initiative’s forecast, issued on Nov 1, projected PM2.5 concentrations to rise to 149µg/m³ by Wednesday, Nov 4 — around 49pc above October’s average. The findings offer a more cautious assessment of the improvement claimed by the provincial government. Punjab Senior Minister Marriyum Aurangzeb had shared data with Dawn in October showing that Lahore’s average US AQI (PM2.5) stood at 180.5 during October 2026, compared with 204.6 in 2025, 213 in 2024 and approximately 193 to 195 in 2022 and 2023. Her data showed that October 2026 was the only year among the five in which the city did not record an AQI above 300, with the highest reading standing at 262 on Oct 31. However, PAQI’s assessment underlines that the improvement was partly weather-driven and that pollution remained above the national health standard throughout the month. With November bringing a fresh deterioration in air quality, the latest readings and satellite fire detections highlight the continuing challenge of controlling agricultural burning and other sources of pollution across Punjab.

Pakistan assumes chairmanship of SCO Interbank Consortium for 2026-27. Pakistan has assumed the chairmanship of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Interbank Consortium (SCO-IBC) for 2026-27, the Ministry of Finance said on Monday. HBL Chairman Sultan Ali Allana has taken over as head of the consortium for the period. “The development coincides with Pakistan’s chairmanship of the SCO for the same period, reflecting the country’s role in promoting regional trade, investment, financial connectivity and economic cooperation”, the statement said. The ministry congratulated Allana on assuming the responsibility and reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitment to strengthening economic partnerships among SCO member states, facilitating cross-border trade and investment, and advancing regional integration and shared prosperity. The SCO-IBC is a key platform for financial collaboration among SCO member states. It aims to promote sustainable development through cooperation with multilateral institutions, enhance regional trade and investment, and explore new mechanisms for developing transnational mega projects. Pakistan is also set to host the next meeting of the SCO Council of Heads of State (CHS) after assuming its chairmanship in September. The development marks another step in the country’s growing engagement with the regional organisation, which has expanded its focus from security cooperation to economic development and regional connectivity. Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar has said Pakistan’s membership of the SCO has evolved from observer status to proactive full membership since 2017, reflecting its commitment to multilateralism and regional cooperation. He has also described Pakistan’s upcoming chairmanship as a reflection of the confidence reposed in its regional and international leadership. Pakistan hosted the SCO Council of Heads of Government meeting in Islamabad in October 2024 and is currently chairing the organisation’s Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure for 2025-26. It also holds the permanent chairmanship of an SCO working group on poverty alleviation, which focuses on improving living standards across the region.

US midterms: Michigan Democrat's endorsement of Republican ruffles critical Senate race. A prominent Michigan Democrat endorsed Republican Mike Rogers on Sunday, giving President Donald Trump’s Republicans an unexpected boost in ​a critical US Senate race two days before midterm elections that will decide control of Congress. US Representative Haley Stevens, who lost the Michigan Democrats’ Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed in a bitterly ‌contested race, publicly backed Rogers and appeared with him at a Detroit church, threatening to worsen divisions in a state viewed as crucial to Democratic hopes of retaking the US Senate. “I don’t belong in Abdul’s campaign,” Stevens said in a video posted to social media. Hours later at a political rally in Iowa, Trump invited Stevens to join the Republican Party. He told reporters beforehand that he would reach out to her to thank her for the endorsement, which he called “a smart thing to do because El-Sayed would destroy our country.” Thirty-five Senate seats and ​all 435 House of Representatives seats are on the ballot on Tuesday. Republicans hold narrow majorities in both chambers. Polls show Democrats are favored to win a majority of the House and are locked in a ​tight battle for control of the Senate, where the outcome likely will rest with a handful of states, including Michigan and Alaska. If Democrats take control of the House or ⁠Senate, they could block Trump’s legislative agenda for his final two years in office and launch investigations of an administration that has so far faced largely compliant Republican majorities. The White House has been preparing to implement portions of Trump’s agenda ​without the aid of Congress, including its tarrif pressure on trading partners. Michigan rift Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers came on the day she was scheduled to appear with El-Sayed in a show of party unity. But the planned event unraveled after Stevens called ​on El-Sayed to condemn an outside group’s ad that she said blames Israel for high grocery prices. “That ad was very painful,” Stevens told CNN on Sunday night. “There are so many Democrats who want to vote for our Democratic nominee, and they’re just being told, ‘Hey, this is a party you don’t belong in, or this is a campaign you don’t belong in.’” El-Sayed’s campaign recently asked Stevens to skip his events through Election Day so as “not to distract from the central issues of the campaign,” a person familiar with the matter said. Republicans sought to capitalise ​on Stevens’ move. “This is courage in politics in America today,” Rogers said. “When you see a party, and at least a sliver of the party, veering off into the virulent hate that they have been spewing toward a group of ​people, it gets dangerous.” Later on Sunday at the Iowa rally, Trump repeated false claims that El-Sayed is a “jihadist” - attacks that fit a broader pattern of inflammatory rhetoric from Trump and other Republicans targeting Arab Americans and Muslims. Stevens’ move did not appear to dent support ‌for El-Sayed. A ⁠New York Times /Siena poll released and partly conducted on Sunday showed the Democratic nominee with a 53 per cent to 42pc lead over Rogers. A spokesperson for El-Sayed’s campaign said that it raised $1.2 million in the four hours after Stevens endorsed Rogers, making it the campaign’s second-best fundraising day since the Democratic primary election in August. He declined to directly address Stevens’ endorsement on Sunday. “This race was never about me,” El-Sayed told MS NOW. “It was never even about Mike Rogers. It’s certainly not about Haley Stevens. This race is about the people in the state of Michigan, the people that I’ve gotten to know in their churches and synagogues, in their basements and their living rooms, talking about what they need and deserve.” A number of ​Stevens’ congressional staff resigned over the endorsement, according to ​reports from CNN and the Hill , while some voters expressed ⁠disdain. “Haley Stevens is a traitor,” said Pamela Johnson, 72, after casting her ballot for El-Sayed in Warren, a Detroit suburb. Alaska Intervention Falters Also on Sunday, the Trump administration’s attempt to intervene in Alaska’s Senate race faltered when a federal judge dismissed the US Justice Department’s lawsuit seeking to block certification of the results if Republican incumbent Senator Dan S. Sullivan narrowly ​loses. The Justice Department argued voters may be confused by the presence of a challenger named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr on the same ballot. The issue has roiled the campaign ​over the last several days after ⁠the New York Times reported that Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign was involved in recruiting Daniel J. Sullivan Jr into the race as a spoiler. The senator said on Sunday he would accept the results of Tuesday’s election even as the Trump administration presses a criminal investigation into the issue. But Alaska Governor Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, has suggested he may not certify a victory by Peltola, and the incumbent Sullivan declined to say whether he would support efforts to refuse certification. He joined his party colleagues in accusing ⁠the other Sullivan ​of trying to confuse voters with his similar name. “They got the decoy guy on the ballot,” the senator told CNN’s “State of the Union” ​program. “I’m sure I’m going to lose a lot of votes to that trickery. So what I say to Alaskans is, ‘Don’t let them get away with the tricks.” Peltola has denied involvement, and Sullivan Jr has denied coordinating with Peltola’s campaign.

Laden with eggs, robots race up sacred Chinese mountain. Dozens of robots took on more than 3,000 steps up one of China’s most famous peaks on Monday, carrying eggs and watermelons in a race organisers billed as a test of real-world machine endurance, state media showed. For hundreds of years, Mount Tai — the tallest peak in China’s eastern Shandong province — was an important pilgrimage for Chinese emperors and features prominently in Chinese mythology. But the rugged terrain would prove a stern test for some competitors. One humanoid robot wearing a bandana collapsed in a heap on the cobbled route before engineers rushed in to repair it, while another tumbled down a flight of stairs and came to rest beside a rubbish bin. The Unesco World Heritage site hosted technologies of the future as part of a new World Mountain Robot Challenge, footage from state broadcaster CCTV showed. Over a 3.9-kilometre course with more than 600 metres of ascent, robots and their engineers from around 90 teams were tasked with either completing the route as fast as possible or transporting fragile goods like fresh eggs and watermelons to the summit. A canine robot made by Beijing Lingyi Technology — a subsidiary of industry giant Unitree — completed the course in 43 minutes, 41 seconds, to win the four-legged speed category. Most tourists take at least two hours to complete the route, according to CCTV . The fastest humanoid robot — belonging to Beijing-based team Zhishen Lingyue — completed a shorter race course in 27 minutes and 26 seconds. Organisers called Mount Tai’s rocky terrain a “natural extreme testing ground” that could help train robots for real-world use, local media reported. The race, organised by the state-run China Media Group, featured cash prizes for winners in several categories, including the fastest robots and the best load-carrying four-legged machine.

Bangladesh garment workers protesting for higher wages clash with police. Thousands of Bangladeshi garment workers blocked a major highway and clashed with police on Monday, demanding a monthly minimum wage more than double their current pay, as protests spread across industrial hubs. The South Asian nation of 170 million people is the world’s second-biggest garment exporter behind China , manufacturing clothes for some of the largest international brands. Hundreds of workers in Gazipur, north of the capital Dhaka, blocked the Dhaka-Tangail highway, vandalising several vehicles, while large groups took to the streets in the Mirpur district, where police dispersed demonstrators with tear gas, AFP reporters saw. Garment workers gather to protest demanding higher minimum wages in Dhaka on November 2, 2026. — AFP Angry workers also set fire to a police vehicle. The protests came despite the government’s announcement on Sunday that it would establish a wage board to review the minimum wage in the vital garment industry, which employs millions of people and generates the bulk of Bangladesh’s export earnings. However, labour leaders say workers’ grievances extend beyond the formation of the board, citing inflation and rising household expenses. The protesters demand a 30,000-taka monthly wage, more than double their current pay. Workers currently earn about 13,000 taka a month, according to Kalpona Akter of the Bangladesh Centre for Workers Solidarity. Police fired stun grenades and tear gas canisters to disperse crowds in Ashulia, a Dhaka suburb and the site of some of the country’s largest factories. Police personnel detain a garment worker during a protest demanding higher minimum wages in Dhaka on November 2, 2026. — AFP “Food prices, cooking gas and electricity bills have all gone up — the government must either bring down the prices of essential commodities or raise our wages,” said Mamum, 28, a factory worker. Machine operator Sharmin, 24, said: “We keep the wheels of the economy turning. They must listen to us.” Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed warned that the government was taking strong action to stop the protests. “Those engaging in unlawful activities and conspiracies under the guise of labour movements will be tackled with an iron hand,” he said after meeting industry leaders on Monday. Police personnel stand guard near the site of garment workers protest demanding higher minimum wages in Dhaka on November 2, 2026. — AFP ‘Crack down’ However, Ahmed also said earlier Prime Minister Tarique Rahman had instructed officials after hosting an emergency cabinet meeting late on Sunday to “ensure workers’ rights and improve their living standards”. He said Rahman had told them to make sure production and exports continued “unhindered”. Bangladesh’s main manufacturer associations for garments and knitwear warned that “prolonged unrest could disrupt production, delay export shipments and affect Bangladesh’s commitments to international buyers”, the state-run BSS news agency said on Monday. Kamrul Hasan, general secretary of the Ekota Garments Sramik Federation, told AFP some labour leaders had gone into hiding. “We were not prepared for this unrest either, as the wage board has already been formed,” he said. “But workers are now protesting over wages and other unresolved issues.” Police personnel stand guard near the site of garment workers protest demanding higher minimum wages in Dhaka on November 2, 2026. — AFP In Ashulia, security officers chased protesters as they scattered down narrow side streets, with the choking tear gas drifting into densely packed housing where families often live crammed into single rooms. “Police fired tear gas shells inside our compound,” said Kamona, 24, who gave only one name. “We have children, but they don’t care.” Industry representatives said workers from at least 529 factories in Dhaka and its surrounding industrial areas, including Savar, Ashulia, Jirani and Gazipur, had left their workplaces on Sunday.

Babar, Shaheen set for Quaid-e-Azam Trophy opening-round clash. Pakistan Test captain Babar Azam and One-day International skipper Shaheen Shah Afridi will headline the opening round of the 69th edition of the Quaid-e-Azam Trophy, which gets under way across Islamabad, Abbottabad and Rawalpindi on Tuesday. Babar will turn out for Lahore Whites, who face Shaheen-led Fata at the Diamond Cricket Ground in Islamabad, in what promises to be one of the early highlights of the premier first-class competition. Several other established Pakistan players will also feature in the tournament, with Saud Shakeel captaining defending champions Karachi Blues, Mohammad Rizwan leading Peshawar Blues and Imam-ul-Haq taking charge of Multan. Abdullah Shafique will captain Sialkot Blues, while Mohammad Nawaz has been named skipper of Rawalpindi in the Silver tier. The Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) on Monday announced the schedule and team rosters for the Gold and Silver competitions, which will run simultaneously and feature 20 regional sides. Eight teams will compete in the Gold tier, with Karachi Blues, Faisalabad, Fata, Lahore Whites, Islamabad, Peshawar Blues, Multan and Sialkot Blues vying for the title. The competition will run from Nov 3 to Dec 12, with the five-day final scheduled for Dec 15-19. The winners will be crowned champions of the 69th edition of the Quaid-e-Azam Trophy, while the 12-team Silver competition will provide a pathway to the top tier for next season. The Silver teams have been divided into two groups of six. Lahore Blues, Rawalpindi, Larkana, Quetta, Bahawalpur and Peshawar Whites form Group ‘A’, while Group ‘B’ comprises Karachi Whites, Azad Jammu and Kashmir, Hyderabad, Dera Murad Jamali, Abbottabad and Sialkot Whites. Group ‘A’ matches will be staged at the KCCA Stadium, SBP and UBL Sports Complexes in Karachi, while Group ‘B’ fixtures will be held at the Multan Cricket Stadium, Sports Complex in Rahim Yar Khan and Dring Stadium in Bahawalpur. The Silver group matches will take place from Nov 3-30, with the final between the two group winners scheduled for Dec 3-7. The winners will earn promotion to the Gold tier for the following season. A total of 60 first-class matches will be played across the two competitions, with 29 fixtures in Gold and 31 in Silver. Both tiers will carry first-class status. The tournament will also mark the first time that Peshawar and Sialkot regions will field two teams each in a first-class competition. In the Gold tier, Lahore Whites’ squad includes Babar, all-rounder Aamir Jamal, Tayyab Tahir and Noman Ali, while Fata will be led by Shaheen and also feature Khushdil Shah and Mohammad Wasim Khan. Karachi Blues, meanwhile, have retained a strong line-up under Saud, with Saim Ayub and Omair Bin Yousuf among the players in their squad. Shan Masood, Abrar Ahmed and Mir Hamza are included in the team’s reserves and national-duty pool. Peshawar Blues will be captained by wicket-keeper batter Rizwan, with Sahibzada Farhan, Mohammad Haris and Iftikhar Ahmed also named in the squad. In the Silver competition, Abbottabad have included Fakhar Zaman and Kamran Ghulam, while Rawalpindi’s squad features Shadab Khan, Haider Ali, Mohammad Nawaz and Jahandad Khan. The PCB said teams would operate with revolving rosters throughout the tournament, with 15 travelling members and the option to draw on reserve players and those in the national-duty pool when available.

Dear Test cricket, I stayed up. Newlands, Cape Town. Saturday morning, before the first ball. Marnus Labuschagne crouches on his haunches at the edge of the outfield, waiting to bat. Australia need 288 to win the Test and the series. In the first innings he made a five-ball duck. He has scored 11 Test hundreds, and the last came at Old Trafford in July 2023. For a stretch he was the best batter in the world. He stands, walks to the middle, and takes guard. He will face three balls. I have not stopped thinking about them. Nothing moved me, so I wrote nothing. Somebody has to move a writer to write… Part One: The Wait Chapter One: Moved Some months earlier I write about this game only when it moves me. Good cricket does not count. Good cricket arrives every week and asks nothing of you. Being moved is rarer: a stranger does something you did not know a person could do, in a country you may never see, at an hour when you should be asleep, and for a few minutes you stop being an audience and become a witness. The first Test of the Ashes did that to me, in two days, and I wrote about it. I watched the other four to the last ball. Then the series ended, an English summer came and went, and I could not name you one innings. Nothing moved me, so I wrote nothing. Somebody has to move a writer to write, and the universe, with its usual disregard for my sleep, took the job. My resistance lasted about one session. Chapter Two: Two Rooms Same city. Same Saturday night In the first room, a performer who has done this show 200 times walks onto a stage built for it. The lighting is rehearsed. The song you came for arrives second, exactly where it was promised. The audience paid for that, and it is delivered to the minute. Nobody leaves disappointed and nobody leaves changed. This is entertainment, and I have nothing against it. Its virtue is that it keeps its word. In the second room, a band walks out with sketches and no plan. In the spring of 1959 Miles Davis brought his musicians into a studio with little more than a handful of scales and melodic outlines, and what they made became the best-selling jazz record of all time. It could have been a mess. The patron in that room knows it could have been a mess, because he has sat through the nights when it was. He pays for the chance to find out. The two audiences differ in more than taste. The first judges the evening against a promise. The second judges himself against the evening: was I paying enough attention to be there when it happened? Entertainment asks whether you enjoyed it. Art asks whether you were awake. Test cricket is the second room, stretched to five days. Part Two: The Match Chapter Three: Tuesday Newlands, day one The series stands at one all. Australia won in Durban by 214, on Matt Renshaw’s 190. South Africa won in Gqeberha by an innings and 31 runs, on Temba Bavuma’s 179. Cape Town decides it. Pat Cummins wins the toss and chooses to field, citing moisture in the pitch. A captain has made that choice at Newlands only 12 times since 1889. The moisture turns out to be a rumour. By lunch Marques Ackerman and Aiden Markram have South Africa at 140 without loss. Ackerman is playing his second Test. He makes 95 off 94 balls, with twelve fours and two sixes, four of the fours in a row off Mitchell Starc. Then, five runs short of a hundred, he walks down the pitch to Nathan Lyon, who has waited 15 years for that look on a batter’s face. Stumped. Afterward Ackerman says he lives by the sword and dies by it, and that he left a hundred out there. He does not pretend to be happy about it. Then Starc. There is a kind of bowler around whom an afternoon changes ownership. Wasim Akram is one. Shane Warne was another. The scoreboard was never the evidence. The evidence was the batter, who knew first. On Tuesday evening Starc joins them. He has Bedingham caught on 50 and, two balls later, Wiaan Mulder, caught behind for a duck. He takes Rickelton and Jansen in a single over with the new ball, then Coetzee and Rabada. South Africa fall from 203 for 1 to 329 all out. Starc finishes with six for 72, his 20th five-wicket haul, and he is not done. Mulder walks off with a zero beside his name. Keep that number. In the last half hour of the day Starc is bowling himself off his feet, and at the start of his 22nd over he reaches down for his right calf and runs in anyway. South African captain Temba Bavuma ducks a bouncer during the third Test against Australia at the Newlands Stadium.–AFP Chapter Four: Wednesday Day two Simon Harmer has Travis Head chopping on for 41. Then Labuschagne, going back to a ball that wanted him forward, edges it to slip, where Aiden Markram takes the catch. Five balls. No runs. He arrived at Newlands needing a score to keep his place, and Australia are 58 for 2. Tuesday, Mulder: nought. Wednesday, Labuschagne: nought. The match sets them side by side and says nothing. I am travelling, and the Test starts at an hour that my body, wherever it thinks it is, cannot place. By the second night I have moved two meetings. By the fourth I have moved the rest. I, who could not spare 10 minutes for cricket since the Ashes, now discover that I have five days. Chapter Five: Friday Day four Thursday belongs to Australia. Josh Inglis makes 102 off 135 balls and, with Alex Carey, who makes 80, adds 185. Australia lead by 100. By the close South Africa are four down and 40 ahead, a lead you could carry in one hand. Friday belongs to two men who have known each other since school. Ryan Rickelton already owns a Test double century and is still the quieter name in a batting order that includes Aiden Markram and Temba Bavuma. Mulder walked off on Tuesday with a zero. Their plan is a lesson in humility. Rickelton has decided to take a few on the body rather than play the short ball, and he does. He spends 37 balls in the 90s. On 92, Starc bangs one in short, Rickelton shoulders arms, and it thuds into his ribs. He lifts his shirt to show Travis Head, at short leg, the bruise coming up, for confirmation or approval. Head, by all accounts, offers both. Rickelton reaches his hundred after tea and finishes on 101 off 219 balls. Then Mulder reverse-sweeps, Josh Inglis dives at backward point to cut it off, and Rickelton is run out, the stumps broken by Labuschagne. The stand is worth 154. It would be easier to say that Mulder rescued South Africa. What he does is odder. He rescues himself, and South Africa happens to be standing next to him. He makes 115 off 221 balls, and on the stroke of stumps he clubs Cummins to deep midwicket, where Mitchell Starc, who has done everything else on this ground for three days, takes the catch. South Africa have 387. Australia need 288. Wiaan Mulder. Tuesday: 0. Friday: 115. The same 387 would have been a decent total on Tuesday. On Friday, on a pitch that has begun to come apart, from a side that was four down the night before, it is a verdict. Nothing else in sport asks you to be brave slowly, and then makes you wait through the night to learn whether it counted. South African all-rounder Wiaan Mulder runs between the wickets.–AFP Chapter Six: Saturday Morning Day five Kagiso Rabada has the new ball. Travis Head takes a single off the second delivery. The third is down the leg side, Matt Renshaw, the hero of Durban, is strangled, and Rickelton takes the catch behind the stumps. A golden duck. Labuschagne gets up off his haunches and walks out. David Warner had predicted that the day would end with Labuschagne a 100 not out and Australia winning with seven wickets down. The first ball Marnus faces runs off the leading edge, past gully, for four. Two balls later Rabada bowls one that nips back. Labuschagne, playing no shot, is hit on the back pad in front of the stumps. Richard Kettleborough raises his finger. Labuschagne reviews. The replay shows the ball clipping the off bail, which makes it umpire’s call, and the original decision stands. Out for four. 5-2. Umpire’s call is a rule written for doubt. If the ball is only clipping the stump, the umpire’s original decision stands, whatever it was. Had Kettleborough shaken his head, the very same replay would have left Labuschagne standing where he was. I have thought about the innings that follows that headshake more than I have thought about most of the ones that were played. It starts the way his best always have, quietly: a leave, a leave, a punch through cover that sounds like a door closing on a bad year. By lunch he is on 30, and Australia, three down, are breathing again. By tea the drought is over. By the close it is a hundred, and Warner’s forecast, which sounded absurd that morning, looks like prophecy. It never happened. I would swear I watched it. This is what faith costs in Test cricket, and what luck pays out. Everything Labuschagne has done since he was a boy, the dawn nets, the leaves, the belief, is weighed in the end against a sliver of bail and one man’s reading of it. Luck is not the opposite of skill in this game. It is the second signature on the contract. A batter can prepare for everything except the sliver, and the sliver is where Test cricket keeps its mystery. I wrote once about Virat Kohli and the fifth stump, that line outside off where a ball extends an invitation and a great batter accepts it against his own training. Kohli was beaten by the ball he should have left. Labuschagne was beaten by the ball he left. The craft is the same and so is the verdict: the sport does not care how well you prepared. I support South Africa. I have rarely been so sorry to see them succeed. By the end of the day Nathan Lyon, at number 10, will have made 33 not out, the top score of the innings, 29 more than a man who was once the best batter in the world. Labuschagne has the application, the talent, the faith and the hours. All of it is still there. And one morning, for no reason anyone can name, it leaves, the way a word does when you say it too many times and it becomes a sound. He may have played his last Test for Australia in that over. I hope not. Marnus Labuschagne. Wednesday: 0. Saturday: 4. Head scores the way a vending machine dispenses: promptly, correctly, and without looking at you. He hits a few boundaries, then edges Rabada to Marco Jansen at gully. 14. It is Rabada’s 350th Test wicket, reached in 13,808 balls, faster than any bowler in history and 911 balls quicker than Dale Steyn. I am alarmed by how much I enjoy it. Simon Harmer comes on in the 12th over, and the morning comes apart. Inglis is run out for four after Cameron Green sets off for a run that was never on, and Ackerman, who left a hundred on the field on Tuesday, takes a wicket back from silly point. Alex Carey reverse-sweeps and top-edges to Jansen. Cooper Connolly is caught behind for nought. Starc, promoted to number eight to deal with the footmarks, survives 25 balls without scoring and is caught at bat-pad off the last ball before lunch, the longest duck of his Test career. At lunch Australia are 60 for 7. Harmer has 3-5 from eight overs. South African spinner Simon Harmer dives to take a catch.–AFP Chapter Seven: Saturday Afternoon Day five, after lunch. After lunch the match stops moving, and it becomes the best thing in it. Australia score two runs in an hour. There is a stretch of 78 balls without a run. Green is sheltered from Harmer’s off breaks, and Cummins, who has come out beside him with a plan to bat time instead of runs, defends everything that comes. Six fielders crouch around the bat. It is a standoff in which the only weapon anyone holds is patience. When the first run finally comes, the Newlands crowd cheers it, ironically and at length. Then Harmer changes ends, drags one through Green’s gate, and Green is bowled for 27. 62-8. And then two men who have no business being dangerous become dangerous. Cummins faces 90 balls and scores 11 runs, and I have never been prouder of a ratio. Nathan Lyon, who bowled 44 overs in South Africa’s second innings, bats as though that were a warm-up. They add 45. The result was settled hours ago. They know it, the crowd knows it, and everyone awake across the world knows it. They stay anyway. This is the strange, magnificent design of the thing. A Test match asks the athlete to bring his best courage and his best stamina not for an hour but for five days. Then, on the fifth afternoon, when the specialists have failed, it hands the match to the people who were hired to do something else. A fast bowler walks out and decides to become a wall. A spinner decides to become a clock. Nothing they do will change the result, and that is exactly why it matters. A win is a fact. This is a gift. When a man spends 90 balls on something that cannot be won, the scoreboard stops being the point, and the rest of us find out what valour looks like once the reward has been taken away. Just before tea Harmer traps Cummins lbw. Cummins reviews. The ball is clipping the off bail, and the umpire’s call stands. It is the second time that day those words have decided a man’s fate, and both times the call goes South Africa’s way. Every great Test victory owes something to luck. Then, with the first ball of his 22nd over, Harmer bowls Josh Hazlewood. Australia are all out for 111. South Africa win by 176. Harmer finishes with 6 for 16 from 21.1 overs, 14 of them maidens, and 10 wickets in the match, the first time he has done that in a Test. He is 37. He bowled through a torn nail on Thursday. He spent years with Essex in English county cricket, was recalled, and on a Saturday in Cape Town takes apart the top-ranked Test side in the world. South African players celebrate a wicket.–AFP Part Three: The Vigil Chapter Eight: Everyone Awake Some hours later. A machine can give you the result of this Test in one line. It will be correct, and it will take four seconds. Australia 111, South Africa by 176, the series 2-1. It cannot tell you what it was like to be awake for it. We are living through a strange subtraction. Answers arrive before the questions are finished. Summaries sit above the thing they summarise. Almost everything that once cost an afternoon now costs a tap, and the cost was never the enemy. The cost was where the meaning was kept. A letter mattered because it took a week. A song mattered because you had to wait for the radio to play it. Take away the wait and you take away the room where the feeling lived. Test cricket is the last large public thing built so that nothing can be skipped. You cannot fast-forward the 90th ball. You cannot be told how it felt. The only way to know is to stay, and staying is the whole price of admission, paid in the oldest currency we have: hours, spent in company. Somewhere in that fifth afternoon, in a time zone that had no business being awake, a stranger was watching Cummins defend a ball for a reason no efficiency expert would accept. Most of us had no stake in the result. We were there because the sport asks a very human question, which is whether you will stay. That is human-centred design. The game is built to the scale of a person. It takes five days because a person needs five days to become who he will be on the fifth. It lets a man fail in public and return in the second innings. It makes 10 team-mates watch each member be afraid, one at a time, and know exactly what it costs. And in an age that can produce the likeness of almost anything, it offers the one thing that cannot be produced: a reason to stay up with strangers for something that may not end well, and to be glad you did. South African players acknowledge the spectators before walking off the field following their win over Australia in the third Test at the Newlands Stadium.–AFP Chapter Nine: Thank You 16 months earlier, and also now. In June 2025 I sat at Lord’s through Rabada’s third-innings spell of the World Test Championship final and watched Bavuma lift the mace. It was South Africa’s first global title in 27 years, and it was the day and the occasion that moved me most that year. That same summer I wrote about a five-Test series and called the piece Five Shades of Flat. Now the same South Africans, under Bavuma, who lost the first Test of this series and won the next two, are the number one Test side in the world for the first time since January 2016. Thank you Test Cricket.. Thank you For lunch, to begin with, which stops a Test match at its most dangerous moment so that twenty-two men can have a civilized meal. For tea, the second truce of the day. For the maiden over, the only unit of achievement in sport defined by nothing happening. For the duck, a zero named after a bird, so that even the worst day a batter can have arrives with a little feathered mercy. For a game in which a man can score eleven in ninety balls and be remembered as a hero, and another can score four in three balls and be mourned. For umpire’s call, in which a machine admits it is not sure. For the nightwatchman, the bad light, the follow-on, the draw that feels like a victory and the victory that feels like a funeral. We could not have invented you. No committee would have approved you. You take five days to say what other sports say in two hours, and you say it better, because you leave room for people to be wrong in public and the time for them to come back. I closed the laptop. The room was quiet, and the quiet was full, the way a house is after the guests have gone. Whether Marnus Labuschagne walks out again for Australia is the one thing this match left unanswered. Test cricket will answer in its own time. I intend to be awake when it does. Yours, awake.. I suspect he is too.

LHC directs jail authorities to arrange meeting between Noreen Niazi, her daughters. LAHORE: The Lahore High Court (LHC) on Monday directed jail authorities to arrange a meeting between Noreen Niazi, the sister of PTI founder Imran Khan, and her two daughters on Tuesday (tomorrow). Justice Abher Gul Khan issued the directives while hearing petitions challenging the extensions in the detention orders of Imran’s sisters Noreen, Uzma Khan and Aleema Khanum. The judge also summoned the Lahore deputy commissioner to appear in person on Nov 4 and explain the extensions in the detention orders of Noreen and Uzma Khan. Aleema and Noreen, along with their sister Uzma Khan, were detained under the Punjab Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance, 1960 in September, as the PTI geared up for a protest march to Islamabad. Their detentions have come amid reports of several PTI leaders and workers being taken into custody ahead of the march planned to demand Imran’s release from prison. Among them, Aleema was detained on Sept 20 for 30 days and Noreen and Uzma the next day for the same period. Their detention was challenged in the court after the 30-day period lapsed last month, following which the Punjab government informed the court that their detention periods had been extended for another 30 days. During Monday’s hearing, the petitioners’ counsel Rana Mudassar Umar told the court that Noreen’s two daughters and lawyers wanted to meet her. He expressed concern over her health, saying she was an elderly woman and her actual condition could only be ascertained after meeting her. Among the three detainees, Noreen had been shifted to the Punjab Institute of Cardiology (PIC) following her deteriorating health, on the recommendation of the doctors of the Kot Lakhpat Jail, where she has been detained. Later, adviser to the prime minister on political affairs, Rana Sanaullah, had informed the Senate that Noreen was fine after being provided medical treatment in Lahore. On Monday, the judge asked a provincial law officer whether a specific day had been fixed for prisoners’ meetings. The law officer said the jail authorities had no objection to allowing the meeting. The law officer also submitted a report on behalf of the Home Department, stating that Noreen had been taken to hospital for treatment and subsequently shifted back to jail on doctors’ advice. He said her daughter, Hajira Niazi, had been allowed to meet her at the hospital on Oct 29. The court subsequently directed the jail authorities to facilitate a meeting between Noreen and her two daughters on Tuesday. Meanwhile, the judge adjourned the hearing of a petition challenging Aleema’s fresh detention until next week. Reports sought Earlier in the day, the LHC had sought reports from the Punjab Home Department. Justice Khan directed the Home Department to submit the reports by 2pm as she heard pleas filed by Noreen’s daughter, Sakeena, and Shahrez Khan, Aleema’s son. The petitioner’s counsel contended that Aleema, Noreen and Uzma’s detentions had been extended “unlawfully”. He noted that after the initial 30-day detention period, the Lahore deputy commissioner had issued a notification for its extension. He claimed that the detained women had also not been allowed to meet their family members or lawyers. The counsel asked the court to declare the fresh detention notifications “illegal”. PTI Secretary General Advocate Salman Akram Raja informed the court that Aleema’s driver had also been detained. He requested the court to show leniency towards the driver, saying his family was deeply distressed. Justice Khan then sought reports from the provincial Home Department and said she would examine the matter after going through the reports.

On eve of midterms, final polls point to Democratic gains, but can Republicans hold the Senate?. Democrats have made significant gains in the final days of the 2026 midterm campaign, with new polls showing them leading in several states that President Donald Trump carried in 2024. The findings point to a changing political landscape, although the outcome of the Senate contests remains uncertain. The final New York Times /Siena College surveys of seven key Senate battlegrounds show Democratic candidates ahead in Michigan , Texas, Kansas, Maine and Ohio. They also hold narrower leads in Alaska and Iowa, where the contests remain highly competitive. The results have attracted particular attention because several of these states have traditionally favoured Republicans. Democratic leads in Texas and Kansas, in particular, would have appeared unlikely only a few months ago. The surveys, released on November 1, covered 5,708 likely voters across the seven states. The individual state surveys had margins of sampling error ranging from approximately 3.3 to 4.8 percentage points.
