Even the larger leads elsewhere remain subject to polling error. The findings nevertheless show how competitive the Senate map has become as both parties seek control of Congress. A Republican warning: The Senate remains competitive The prospect of Democratic gains is no longer being acknowledged only by Democratic strategists or traditionally liberal media outlets. Fox News , which generally offers a more favourable perspective on Republican electoral prospects, has also revised its assessments. In its November 1 Power Rankings, Fox moved Kansas from “Lean Republican” to “Toss-up”, acknowledging that the Republican incumbent was facing a serious challenge in a traditionally conservative state. Of the 100 seats in the Senate, Fox considers Democrats favoured in 48 Senate seats and Republicans in 45, with seven competitive states likely to determine control of the chamber. It nevertheless describes the overall Senate contest as a toss-up. Its reasoning is based largely on electoral geography. Trump carried seven of the 11 battleground states in 2024, several by double-digit margins. Republicans believe that voters who supported him in those states could return to the polls and support Republican Senate candidates, even if the national political environment has shifted. Fox also points to the number of undecided voters in Alaska, Iowa and Kansas. A late movement towards Republican candidates, combined with strong Election Day participation, could change the outcome. The network’s analysis presents two possible scenarios: a Democratic gain that could give the party as many as 55 Senate seats, or a Republican performance strong enough to preserve a majority of up to 52. Either party needs to secure 51 seats in the Senate for a majority win. The House picture is different. Fox ’s final Power Rankings project that Democrats are likely to win at least 223 seats, with the possibility of reaching 240 in a strong performance. In the lower House of Representatives, the winner needs to gain at least 218 out of the 435 voting seats. Other forecasts examine the changing political map. The Wall Street Journal , reporting on the latest assessment by the Cook Political Report, said Democrats had become slight favourites to capture the Senate. Cook identifies seven Senate races — Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas — as sufficiently competitive to remain within the margin of error. For the House, Cook projects Democratic gains of between 12 and 25 seats, potentially giving the party a majority of as many as 240 members. Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Dr. Abdul El-Sayed greets supporters at the “Knock Out the Vote Rally” on November 1, 2026 in Southfield, Michigan. —Getty Images via AFP CBS News has also reported a sustained Democratic advantage in its House modelling. Its October 25 analysis, however, offered an important qualification: the Democratic lead had remained relatively stable rather than expanding, and voters who were still uncertain about participating tended to lean more Republican. That distinction matters. A favourable polling environment does not necessarily mean that all voters expressing dissatisfaction with the administration will turn out on Election Day. The Harvard model assigns probabilities to a possible Democratic takeover. A forecast from the Harvard ElectIt project offers another way of assessing the congressional contests. The project provides three versions of its 2026 forecast: one based on its statistical election model, a second incorporating national generic-ballot polling and a third incorporating available state and district polls. The underlying LogisTiCC model uses historical congressional election results and accounts for factors including incumbency, candidate-specific effects, strategic departures from office and the historical tendency of the president’s party to lose ground in midterm elections. The poll-based versions adjust the model using additional polling information. Under the forecast configuration displayed in the Harvard link used for this report, Democrats have a 96pc probability of taking the House and a 79pc probability of gaining control of the Senate. The model projects approximately 241 Democratic House seats, a net gain of 26, and 53 Democratic Senate seats, an increase of six. The reported 95pc ranges are wide: 214 to 282 seats in the House and 47 to 57 in the Senate. These ranges underline that the figures are statistical estimates, not guaranteed outcomes. The Senate projection is particularly significant because it illustrates how the model evaluates the possibility of Democrats overcoming the geographical disadvantages that have traditionally made the chamber difficult for them to capture. The Harvard project cautions against treating a single projected seat count as a certain result. Its different forecast versions can produce different estimates as polling information changes. Progressive politics and the changing Democratic coalition The emerging political picture also reflects a longer evolution within the Democratic Party, particularly the growth of progressive politics and dissatisfaction with established political institutions. Commentator Zeeshan Shah, a physician in Northern Virginia, believes Senator Bernie Sanders helped inject new energy into the progressive movement, creating political space for candidates challenging the Republican establishment. After Sanders came New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani , who is believed to have taken that energy into the mainstream by directly challenging Trump and the politics associated with his administration, according to Mohsin Masood, a Virginia educationist. Political science professor Farhat Haq believes Democrats could benefit from another pendulum swing in American politics, driven largely by dissatisfaction with Trump. US President Donald Trump arrives to speak at a midterm campaign rally at Five Flags Center in Dubuque, Iowa on November 1, 2026. —AFP She points to rising living costs, the war involving Iran and the Gaza conflict as factors contributing to public discontent. Haq links the economic consequences of the Iran war to inflation and the pressure on household budgets. She also argues that Trump has lost support among some of the groups that helped him politically, including Latino voters . Haq notes that PTI supporters in the United States, despite remaining politically active, are no longer supporting Trump as they did previously. Together, these assessments suggest that the political shift may reflect more than the immediate circumstances of the campaign. Economic anxiety, foreign-policy disagreements and disappointment with established political leadership have all entered the debate over the direction of the country. The final test comes on Tuesday Republicans currently hold a 53-47 Senate majority, including two independents who caucus with Democrats. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to secure an outright 51-seat majority. The House is a more straightforward target. Republicans hold a narrow majority, and the latest polling and election ratings point to a highly competitive contest for control. A change in either chamber would significantly affect Trump’s ability to advance his legislative programme. Democratic control would also give the opposition party greater authority to investigate the administration and scrutinise its policies. The final polls and forecasts show Democrats entering Election Day with opportunities in several states and congressional districts that were not widely expected to be competitive earlier in the campaign. Yet polling error cannot be dismissed. Undecided voters, differences in turnout and the difficulty of predicting who will actually vote can all produce results that diverge from final surveys. For Democrats, the election offers an opportunity to regain the House and potentially the Senate as well. For Republicans, the task is to persuade their supporters that the contests remain open and to ensure that voters who have not participated early turn out on Tuesday. The final results will show whether the patterns identified by the polls and forecasting models were temporary expressions of dissatisfaction or evidence of a broader change in American electoral politics.

Pakistan fined for slow over-rate in tri-series final. Pakistan have been fined five per cent of their match fees for maintaining a slow over-rate during their three-wicket victory over Sri Lanka in the One-day International tri-series final in Lahore on Saturday. The hosts were found to be one over short after time allowances were taken into consideration by match referee Jeff Crowe of the Emirates ICC Elite Panel, the International Cricket Council said in a statement on Monday. Pakistan captain Shaheen Shah Afridi pleaded guilty to the offence and accepted the proposed sanction, which was imposed under Article 2.22 of the ICC Code of Conduct for Players and Player Support Personnel. The provision stipulates a fine of five per cent of a player’s match fee for every over his side fails to bowl within the allotted time. The charge was levelled by on-field umpires Ahsan Raza and Wayne Knights, third umpire Sharfuddoula Ibne Shahid and fourth umpire Rashid Riaz. Pakistan had conceded 325-8 in the final before chasing down the target of 326 with three wickets and nine balls to spare, securing the tri-series title in front of their home crowd at Gaddafi Stadium. Fakhar Zaman led the successful chase with 127 off 99 balls, hitting 11 fours and six sixes to register his 12th ODI century. His innings helped Pakistan recover from an early collapse and complete a joint-record successful chase in an ODI final.

Consumer inflation falls to 9.6pc in Oct from 10.3pc in Sept. ISLAMABAD: Consumer inflation eased to 9.6 per cent in October from 10.3pc a month earlier , mainly due to a slight slowdown in perishable food products, the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics said on Monday. The slowdown in the inflation rate for the second consecutive month, measured by the Consumer Price Index, reversed the sharp increase recorded in August , when higher food and energy prices pushed the annual rate to 11.1pc from 9.2pc in July. The easing was recorded in both places, in rural areas where inflation fell to 9.5pc from 10.1pc, while urban inflation edged down to 9.8pc from 10.5pc. The October reading was also within the Ministry of Finance’s projection of 9.5pc to 10.5pc for the month in its Monthly Economic Update and Outlook for October . According to the finance ministry, easing headline inflation offers some relief, while improved crop supplies can help ease food price pressures. However, despite the decline in the annual rate, prices rose 1.1pc month-on-month in October. The annual inflation rate was 6.2pc in October last year. The average inflation between July and October stood at 10.05pc compared with 4.79pc over the corresponding period last year. The easing was largely driven by perishable food prices. Food inflation dropped to 7.8pc in urban areas in October from 8.1pc in September. The decline was much sharper in rural areas, where food inflation fell to 7.1pc from 7.7pc a month earlier. However, non-food inflation moved in the opposite direction, indicating continued pressure on household expenses. Urban non-food inflation decelerated to 10.6pc from 11.5pc in September, while rural non-food inflation fell to 12.3pc from 13.1pc. The latest data shows that the composition of inflation shifted in October. While food inflation slowed sharply, electricity and transport costs continued to rise. Electricity charges increased by 8.50pc from the previous month, while transport prices rose by 30.39pc in urban areas. At the national level, transport costs increased by 1.79pc during October from the previous month and were 28.61pc higher than in the same month last year. Housing, water, electricity, gas and fuels increased by 0.25pc during the month and by 11.03pc on an annual basis. Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy components, also eased slightly. It stood at 7.8pc in urban areas in October, compared with 8.6pc in September, while the rural rate declined to 7.1pc from 8.1pc.

Civilian convicted of offences against state cannot claim fundamental rights, govt says in report to LHC. LAHORE: The Punjab government on Monday informed the Lahore High Court (LHC) that a civilian who commits an offence against the state and is convicted cannot claim the protection of fundamental rights. The response came as the government sought the dismissal of a petition filed by Barrister Hassaan Khan Niazi, nephew of PTI founder Imran Khan, challenging his handover to the army and subsequent trial in a case related to the May 9 riots. In a report submitted after almost a year on behalf of the provincial government through the home secretary and the inspector general of police, the deputy inspector general of police (legal) said every citizen’s first duty was loyalty to the state, citing a 2005 LHC judgment (PLD 2005 LAH 721). The report described Niazi as a convicted prisoner, arguing that his release through a second round of litigation, other than by way of appeal, was not permissible. It said no judicial order was required for his handover because Niazi was neither in judicial custody nor on remand. The report further stated that he was an absconder, unlike the 16 co-accused whose transfer had been sought from an anti-terrorism court while they were in jail. The Sarwar Road station house officer neither handed over Niazi’s custody nor received a letter from the commanding officer, the report added. “That was done by the investigation in-charge of the Sarwar Road police station, who is not a party to the petition,” the report claimed. It stated that the Supreme Court’s May 7, 2025, ruling on the intra-court appeals upheld military trials while granting the accused the right to appeal, but not the right to file constitutional petitions. It said Niazi had already filed an appeal under Section 133-B of the Pakistan Army Act, 1952. “It is a well-established principle that the same question of law cannot be challenged in two different forums simultaneously; therefore, this petition lacks maintainability in the eyes of the law,” the report maintained. It further argued that Niazi had misread the Supreme Court’s short order, which applied only to petitions pending or filed against anti-terrorism court orders. It accused him of concealing facts about his appeal, his father Hafeezullah Khan Niazi’s earlier proceedings, including a petition before the apex court and a contempt petition, as well as the anti-terrorism court’s May 25, 2023, order. The report said Niazi had not annexed the military court’s order, an objection upheld by the high court in two other petitions. It prayed the court to dismiss the petition on the grounds that it was devoid of merit and not maintainable. According to the report, Niazi was a proclaimed offender in FIR No. 96/2023, registered on May 10, 2023, at the Sarwar Road police station in Lahore Cantonment in connection with an attack on Jinnah House, which was also the residence of the Lahore Corps commander. Police arrested Niazi in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa on Aug 16, 2023. The next day, the commanding officer of the 54 Electrical and Mechanical Engineers Battalion, Lahore, asked for his custody, saying his alleged offences fell under the Official Secrets Act, 1923 and the Pakistan Army Act, 1952 and were triable by court-martial. Police handed him over under Section 76 of the Army Act, read with Section 549(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. He was later sentenced to ten years’ imprisonment in December 2024. Defence ministry’s reply The defence ministry told the LHC that Niazi went to Jinnah House on May 9, 2023, where he made videos and passed sarcastic remarks about the Corps Commander’s uniform. “The incident impacted the image of Pakistan and was prejudicial to the safety and interest of the state,” said a reply signed by an assistant judge advocate general, the army’s legal branch at Headquarters 4 Corps, and filed through an additional attorney general. The reply said that Niazi, held at Kot Lakhpat Jail, was convicted by a Field General Court Martial (FGCM) and sentenced to 10 years’ rigorous imprisonment under Section 3 of the Official Secrets Act, 1923, read with Section 59 of the Army Act. It argued that the petition was barred by Articles 199(3) and 8(3) of the Constitution, xcludes matters related to the proceedings of the armed forces personnel from the purview of the high courts, and that Niazi already had an appeal pending under Section 133-B of the Army Act before the army court of appeals. It said the SC’s May 7, 2025 short order restored Sections 2(1)(d) and 59(4) of the Army Act without striking down Section 133-B. The direction that high courts decide petitions “on their own merits”, the reply said, is not a blanket exemption from the constitutional bar. It said Niazi was tried with a counsel of his choice and made a judicial confession before a magistrate that he did not retract at trial. It said the trial ended on Jan 5, 2024 and he was admitted to Lahore’s Central Jail on Dec 26, 2024. It also argued that he had waited nearly two years before coming to court. The defence ministry’s reply pointed out that Niazi was taken into military custody under Section 549(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. It denied discrimination under Article 25, saying that protesters involved in ordinary disruption were tried by the antiterrorism courts, whereas Niazi’s alleged offence involved a prohibited military installation. A joint trial with the ordinary accused was legally impossible, it said, adding that no Official Secrets Act case had gone to an ordinary court so far. It added that weekly phone calls and meetings with Niazi’s family were arranged after the handover. The ministry asked the court to dismiss the petition as premature, not maintainable and without merit, pleading that the Constitution barred the high court from hearing cases involving persons subject to the Pakistan Army Act, 1952.

Govt enlists oil refineries to shield citizens from global price hikes. The government said on Monday that oil refineries would bear a burden of approximately Rs15 billion each month, which would allow petrol to be sold Rs15 cheaper than what it was in the global market amid the US-Israeli war on Iran. The statement came at a press conference in Islamabad addressed by Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik and Information Minister Attaullah Tarar. Addressing the conference, Malik said that Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif had made efforts to meet with oil refineries and consult with them regarding interventions to ensure that people got the cheapest petrol amid impending steep fuel price increases, including an increase of about Rs15 that would have taken effect on Friday. “I am grateful to all the refineries that saw the public is in difficulty and with the government’s help … increased their throughput,” the minister said, adding that these refineries had made profits from this throughput in the last three months. “They were requested to take a step to support the public during this difficult time, and I am glad that they listened to us … the Rs15 increase that was coming in the petrol prices on Friday, they helped the government with that. Because of that we were able to maintain the price.” He added that more improvement would be seen by the public, expressing his gratitude to the refineries for standing with the government to provide assistance to the public during a time that had caused everyone difficulties — even the government as it struggled to procure oil at increasing prices. As a result of this step, he highlighted, a load of approximately Rs15 billion a month would be borne by these refineries, allowing petrol to be sold at a rate Rs15 per litre cheaper than what it would be in the international market. He expressed his hope that the crisis in the Middle East would soon move towards a peace agreement and that the government could advance with its purposes of “taking the system towards improvement, deregulation and refinery upgrades”. “The government doesn’t want to be cruel to anyone,” Malik stressed, saying that it intended to take actions “with consultations, keeping the public’s interests in mind, in a fair way”. He added that before the crisis, the premium of the refineries was $5 per barrel, and even today a $20 limit had been established. He further said that the government would have to step in and protect the public in case of further difficulties. Tarar also addressed the conference, noting that the premier’s vision “from the first day” had been to put as little burden on the country as possible. He said that even though the situation in the Middle East had affected every economy, including that of Pakistan, “our macroeconomic indicators have remained largely stable — Pakistan’s economy hasn’t taken as much of a hit as other countries”. Regarding Friday’s situation, when petrol prices were increasing in the international market, he said that PM Shehbaz had directed refineries to absorb the price hike in order to prevent the Rs15 increase. “During this difficult time … I think this is a great effort, as a result of which the public has been saved from this difficulty,” the information minister said. He also discussed the fuel subsidy scheme announced by the premier on Sept 13, saying: “If you told me two months ago that there would be a scheme in which, upon SMS registration, motorcycle users get a weekly concession of Rs500 on petrol, and 800cc car users, every 10 days, get 10 litres of petrol for Rs100 less per litre, then I would have told you that it’s probably not possible to implement such a scheme.” He praised PM Shehbaz’s “will power, intent and empathy for the public” that served as the foundation for the scheme. Tarar highlighted that the number of unique users who had registered for the scheme had now crossed 15 million. He said that about Rs27bn had so far been allocated towards this relief and highlighted its success. “This is a unique relief that is not available in the rest of the world,” he said, referring to both the fuel subsidy scheme and the steps taken by the government to prevent the increase in prices on Friday. Answering questions, Malik said that he was the “biggest advocate for deregulation” and for bringing competition into sectors, seeing it as the way to protect people’s welfare and deliver good service. However, he pointed out, “Have you seen any incident in the last 50 years that has been happening in the last six to eight months? What rules-based order do you want to adopt in the middle of this disaster?” He stressed that once the crisis in the region ended, the government would make efforts to return to deregulation; however, currently the focus was on public relief. The two ministers also stressed that there was no fuel shortage and that the country’s needs were being met even during difficult times. Malik said that November’s supply was fully covered, while decisions would be taken on supplies for the winter months of December and January and the prime minister had directed any necessary steps to be taken to ensure supplies. The price of high speed diesel has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on Feb 28. The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March. The government has reintroduced a raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm, and fuel allocations for official vehicles have been cut by 50 per cent for three months. As of July, fuel prices are now fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices.

Political committee denies 'factionalism' within PTI, warns against violating party discipline. PTI on Monday clarified that there was no “factionalism” or “division” within the party and warned of action against any member who violates the party discipline or policy. The warning was issued by PTI’s political committee, which deliberated on party matters and the country’s overall situation. The meeting also discussed the imprisonment of PTI founder Imran Khan and his family members, arrests of party leaders and workers, as well as issues related to its key leaders in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. According to a statement shared on X, the political committee clarified there “is no grouping or division in the party”. “The entire party is united with Imran Khan’s leadership, his ideology and his mission. Putting aside political differences, all party leaders and workers will continue to struggle for common goals,” the statement read. Deeming it “extremely essential to maintain party discipline during this difficult political situation”, the committee decided that “action will be taken under uniform principles against any individual who violates the party’s established discipline and policy”. “The political committee emphasised that parliamentarians, the party’s parliamentary group, and other relevant stakeholders should be fully involved in the consultation process.” Noting the importance of communication with all stakeholders, the committee affirmed that parliamentarians’ suggestions and reservations would be “given special importance”. It also warned that “irresponsible statements” and violations of organisational discipline that deviated from PTI’s platform would not be overlooked. “Strict compliance with the rules will be ensured in this regard so that unity, solidarity, and organisational stability within the party are maintained,” the statement asserted. It was further decided that the party’s future strategy and upcoming course of action will be finalised at the earliest and presented before the workers and the public. The committee reaffirmed its determination to continue its struggle for public rights, democracy and constitutional supremacy despite “ongoing political pressure”. The political committee’s statement follows reported disagreements within PTI over its handling of current challenges, as well as rumours of a group of KP MPAs endorsing Ali Amin Gandapur as the acting provincial president in absence of Junaid Akbar. However, PTI later clarified that Akbar remained the party’s president for KP and named Senator Noorul Haq Qadri to take over his duties in his absence. Last week, several PTI leaders also questioned the party’s decisions and overreliance on Sohail Afridi, the KP CM whose role is non-functional after governor’s rule was imposed in his province. Arrests and detentions The political committee also demanded the release of Afridi, KP Assembly Speaker Babar Saleem Swati and other MPAs who were detained when governor’s rule and emergency were imposed in the province on Oct 11. Governor Faisal Karim Kundi has said Afridi and Swati were placed under house arrest . “Keeping elected public representatives in custody is an insult to democratic values and the public mandate,” the committee declared, according to the statement. It also expressed its concern over reports regarding the transfer of Imran and his wife, Bushra Bibi, to the hospital without “taking the family into confidence”. “Not informing [their] families in a timely manner is contrary to fundamental human rights and legal requirements,” the statement read. The political committee further demanded that the Supreme Court’s orders regarding Imran’s medical treatment be implemented “immediately and fully”, that his family be regularly informed about his health, and that facilities for family meetings be provided. It also sought appropriate medical facilities and meetings with family for Bushra Bibi. The committee went on to demand the immediate release of Imran’s three sisters — Aleema Khan , Noreen Niazi and Uzma Khan — who have remained detained since late September under the Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance (MPO). The committee demanded permission for them to meet and visit Imran. “Depriving the family of their basic right to inquire about their loved one’s well-being and to meet them is unacceptable,” it contended. The committee also expressed “serious” reservations over the alleged arrests of party leaders and workers, particularly actions taken under MPO, and urged that no one be “targeted for revenge on the basis of political differences”. The political committee also condemned alleged raids at residences of former opposition leader Omar Ayub Khan, Sher Ali Arbab, Shah Ahad, and other party leaders, describing them as a “reprehensible” act. On terrorism and economy Discussing the country’s overall situation, PTI’s political committee termed terrorism a “national scourge, for whose eradication effective and serious measrures are unavoidable”. “The protection of citizens’ lives and property is the state’s primary responsibility,” the statement read. However, the committee emphasised that “actions against terrorism should not be used for political vendettas”. “Along with establishing peace and security, the protection of the basic rights of political workers, the public, and supporters of opposing political parties must also be ensured,” it added. When imposing governor’s rule and emergency in KP, the federal government had cited the PTI-led KP government’s “deliberate disengagement” from the fight against terrorism. Federal ministers had even accused the party of supporting terrorists, which PTI strongly denied. Per the statement, the political committee also voiced its concern over rising inflation, prices of petroleum products, and “heavy” electricity bills. While short-term inflation rose to 11.32 per cent year-on-year in the week ending on Oct 29, consumer inflation eased to 9.6pc in October from 10.3pc in September. Heightened petroleum prices due to tensions in the Middle East have also added to inflationary pressures. “The political committee stated that government policies have made the life of the common man unbearable,” said the statement. “The poor and middle classes are already unable to manage their households on limited incomes, while increases in the costs of essential food items, transportation, and energy have multiplied the public’s hardships many times over,” it added. The committee also expressed concern over the market rate of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), noting it was being sold for up to Rs700 per kilogramme, despite the official price being Rs238 per kg. “The relevant authorities should immediately take notice of this disparity, investigate the prices, and take action against profiteering,” the statement asserted, terming it a “grave injustice” to the public. The political committee demanded for the public to be provided with “genuine” relief in the prices of petroleum products and electricity. It also demanded for “hefty” electricity bills, along with the prices of essential commodities, including LPG, to be brought “within the reach of the common man”. “It is the government’s responsibility to free the people from inflation, not to make it difficult for them even to secure two meals a day,” the statement said.

PM directs no leniency for banks slow in providing loans to farmers, SMEs. Prime Minister Shahbaz Sharif on Monday directed that no leniency should be shown to banks who were slow in providing loans to farmers, small and medium enterprises (SMEs), and consumers under the Prime Minister’s Apna Ghar Scheme. The scheme was launched by the prime minister in April, under which housing and construction loans of up Rs10 million were to be given on easy instalments. In a handout issued by the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) on Monday, the prime minister chaired a review meeting on facilitating the provision of loans to priority sectors. “Improving the economy through the development of SMEs, housing, and agriculture and providing employment to youth is the government’s top priority,” PM Shehbaz was quoted as saying. He added that banks demonstrating good performance in the easy provision of loans to agriculture, housing, and SMEs under government initiatives are commendable. “No leniency should be shown by the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) and the Ministry of Finance toward banks showing adopting a slow pace in providing loans to farmers, SMEs, and consumers under the Prime Minister’s Apna Ghar Scheme as per government initiatives,” PM Shehbaz stressed. “Banks are key for the development of the private sector,” the prime minister said. He added that they were expected to extend the same cooperation in the provision of loans for priority sectors as the cooperation the government and government institutions extended to them. “SMEs have the full potential to drive economic growth, promote exports, and create employment opportunities,” PM Shehbaz emphasised. He underlined that the agriculture sector served as the backbone of the national economy, and efforts were underway to increase exports through value addition of agricultural commodities. “The Prime Minister’s Apna Ghar Scheme will boost several industries associated with the housing and construction sector,” the prime minister affirmed. According to the handout, the prime minister directed the finance minister to resolve “financing-related issues for stakeholders in the SMEs sector, agriculture, housing and to prepare a comprehensive action plan”. He further instructed the SBP and Federal Board of Revenue to jointly resolve “tax issues for SMEs and exporters, as well as to develop a comprehensive strategy for risk coverage to facilitate easy loan provision to SMEs”. The statement further said that the meeting was informed that the SBP was working on three fundamental pillars to increase the provision of loans to priority sectors, including improvements in regulations, risk and cost-sharing partnerships between the government and banks and the promotion of digital facilities. It said that a digital portal had recently been launched, through which businesspersons would be able to apply for loans and track the progress of their applications. The meeting was briefed that significant progress had been made by the SBP in providing loans on a priority basis to housing, agriculture, and SMEs. It said that under the Prime Minister’s Apna Ghar Scheme, loans worth Rs511 billion have been approved up to October 23. It added that 86,899 loans have been approved and 15,584 applicants have been disbursed loans worth Rs91bn. In the housing finance sector, the total volume of loans has reached Rs455bn, and the number of beneficiary borrowers has risen to 187,317, the statement said. “The meeting was informed that in the agricultural sector, the loan volume stands at Rs1,329bn, with nearly 3.5 million beneficiaries, while in the SMEs sector, the loan volume is Rs1,148bn and the number of businesspersons obtaining loans has reached 342,458,” the handout said. The briefing stated that targets have been set to increase the loan volume in the agricultural and SME sectors to Rs1,500bn by the end of current fiscal year, it informed. “The meeting was told that risk-sharing and credit-guarantee initiatives have also been introduced by the government for the housing, agriculture and SME sectors, while work is also ongoing on simplifying the procedure for obtaining loans, reducing required documentation and improving access to financial resources through a digital system,” the statement said.

CDF Munir discusses 'evolving regional, international security dynamics' with Chinese dignitary. Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir on Monday discussed “evolving regional and international security dynamics and bilateral relations” with a visiting dignitary from China, the military’s media wing said . According to a statement by Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), Liu Haixing, minister of the International Department of the Communist Party of China’s Central Committee ( IDCPC ), called on CDF Munir at General Headquarters in Rawalpindi. The department is in charge of the CPC’s external relations. Besides discussing matters of mutual interest, both sides “expressed their shared resolve to further strengthen the all-weather strategic cooperative partnership between Pakistan and China”, ISPR said. CDF Munir highlighted the “historic and time-tested bond between the two countries and emphasised the importance of sustained high-level engagement, stronger institutional linkages and expanded cooperation across areas of mutual interest”. China’s Haixing appreciated Pakistan’s contributions to regional peace and stability and expressed confidence in further advancing the longstanding strategic partnership between the two countries, according to the statement. Dar meets Chinese minister Separately, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar also held a bilateral meeting with the IDCPC minister in Islamabad. The Chinese dignitary conveyed greetings from FM Wang Yi, which DPM Dar “warmly reciprocated”, according to the Foreign Office (FO). On his part, Dar also conveyed “warm greetings” to President Xi Jinping on behalf of Pakistan’s leadership. He also reaffirmed Islamabad’s “continued commitment to further strengthening the All-Weather Strategic Cooperative Partnership” with Beijing. “The two sides discussed ways to enhance cultural ties and people-to-people exchanges,” FO added. Both leaders, according to FO, expressed their resolve to maintain close coordination and carry forward the “positive momentum” in bilateral relations. Recently, Pakistan and China signed an agreement to operationalise a green channel at the Sost-Khunjerab border for agricultural and allied products to facilitate bilateral trade. Khunjerab Pass connects Gilgit-Baltistan with China’s Xinjiang region and is the highest paved international border at 15,500 feet above sea level. Also last week, the two countries launched the China-Pakistan Information Corridor (CPIC), which will be based on four pillars — media, business and enterprises, think tanks, and culture/tourism. Pakistan and China share a longstanding strategic partnership rooted in mutual trust, economic cooperation and regional connectivity. Over the decades, ties have expanded across various sectors — including trade, energy, defence, infrastructure and space — with the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) symbolising a shared vision for development.

China calls for Middle East dialogue in talks with Iran, Saudi Arabia, Oman. China stepped up diplomatic efforts on Monday to resolve the Middle East crisis, urging a return to the negotiating table in back-to-back meetings with Iranian, Omani and Saudi officials in Beijing. The meetings come days after United States President Donald Trump issued a fresh war threat more than eight months into the conflict , which was triggered by US-Israeli strikes on Iran and has at times spilled over into neighbouring countries. Beijing supports Tehran in “safeguarding its own sovereignty and security”, Foreign Minister Wang Yi told Ali Bagheri Kani, the deputy secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, according to a Chinese statement. Wang later called for dialogue to end the conflict “while safeguarding regional energy security and the safety of shipping lanes”, as he met with Saudi National Security Adviser Musaad bin Mohammad al-Aiban. China, a top economic partner of Iran, has long sought a detente in the months-long conflict that has disrupted global shipping. Trump said on Saturday that the United States had knocked out much of Iran’s military but still has to “take care of” one or two targets, with Tehran warning of reprisals if attacked. “All parties should… in a spirit of reason and pragmatism, focus on a political solution rather than once again resorting to armed conflict,” Wang told Bagheri Kani, according to the statement. China’s foreign ministry had not previously announced the visit by Bagheri Kani to Beijing. President Xi Jinping also met Oman’s sultan for talks in Beijing on Monday — the first visit to China by the Gulf nation’s head of state since diplomatic ties were established. Xi told Haitham bin Tariq that China was ready to “contribute to peace, stability and prosperity in the region”. The Chinese leader said that the Middle East should not become a “wrestling ground for major-country rivalry and geopolitical conflicts”, state news agency Xinhua reported. Later this month, Beijing will send its Middle East envoy to Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia as part of “shuttle diplomacy visits… aimed at promoting peace talks (and) easing tensions”, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson told a news briefing.

Fridge cyberattack hits supermarkets across Europe. Grocery stores in at least five European countries saw temperatures in their cold cases soar on Monday, with several confirming they had been hit by a cyberattack similar to one three weeks ago in France. Supermarkets in Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Luxembourg and Sweden were among those affected in the latest hacker attack. Major French retailers said on Oct 12 that hundreds of store refrigeration systems were hit by a cyberattack, which forced them to throw out spoiled food and raised concerns about food security. No one has claimed responsibility for either attack. Carrefour Belgium on Monday reported disruption in about 15 of its 700 stores. “It’s a cyberattack; there is no other reason,” said spokesman Mich Vergauwen. An Ikea Belgium spokeswoman likewise said a cyberattack hit its store in Mons, southwestern Belgium, causing the temperature of freezers to rise suddenly in the early hours of Monday. Chains Delhaize, Colruyt and Intermarche also experienced technical problems affecting their fridges in Belgium, while Delhaize reported that four of its stores in Luxembourg were also affected. Belgian industrial refrigeration group Sabcobel said it had begun securing its installations after the Oct 12 attack in France, but around 10 per cent were still not fixed, and some were in the shops affected on Monday. “If Sabcobel hadn’t started this operation … the impact would have been much more important,” chief executive Stephan Moelans told AFP . In Sweden, chain Coop confirmed six of its around 800 stores had been hit by a cyberattack early Monday. “We can confirm that it is a cyber incident. The problem has now been resolved, and the fridges and freezers are working as normal,” spokesman Carlos Cancino told AFP . He said Coop did not know who was behind the attack, but noted that the six affected stores had been connected to a 4G mobile network, not the updated 5G system, which made them “more exposed” to hackers. ‘Vulnerabilities’ Swedish chain Ica also said “a limited number” of its stores experienced refrigeration problems, but the group could not confirm a cyberattack was the cause. According to Ica spokesperson Helena Johansson, the affected stores were all connected to an external refrigeration control system provided by Danish manufacturer Danfoss — the same supplier targeted in the Oct 12 cyberattack on French retailers. She referred all queries to Danfoss. It has not responded to AFP ’s request for a comment. One Ica store located in Sjobo, in southern Sweden, posted on Facebook that its fridges and freezers had “been hacked and they set the temperature at 50 degrees” Celsius. In Finland, irregular temperatures had also been detected in a few smaller grocery stores belonging to the Kesko group. “We are currently investigating the cause, and interference via the network has not yet been ruled out,” Petri Kayhko, head of Kesko’s corporate security, told AFP . Roni Kokkola, an information security specialist at the National Cyber Security Centre at Finland’s Transport and Communications Agency Traficom, would not rule out cyber interference “as far as Finland is concerned”. “We’ve seen this in Europe in the past few months, so it spreading beyond France to other countries has been expected,” he told AFP . “Nowadays it’s very typical that all kinds of vulnerabilities are being exploited ever more actively and rapidly.” In Estonia, at least one supermarket was attacked by hackers who raised the temperature in the refrigeration units to 50°C, public broadcaster ERR reported. The units were older models delivered by Danfoss, similar to the ones targeted in the France attack, Jann Mutso, director of Kitman Coldtech, a manufacturer and distributor of advanced refrigeration systems, told ERR . “The handwriting is the same, but I can’t say more,” Mutso said. Following the attack in France, Danfoss told AFP that most of the affected equipment were “legacy” products which “no longer receive software or security updates”. EU food and agriculture commissioner Christophe Hansen said at the time that “food security requires more attention at all levels”. The “exploitation of food” was now a “reality”, he added.

Adrian Hamilton-Manns appointed new PIA chief executive officer. The board of Pakistan International Airlines (PIA) on Monday announced the appointment of Adrian Hamilton-Manns as its chief executive officer (CEO). In a press release, PIA said Hamilton-Manns “brings a wealth of leadership and strategic experience within the global aviation sector”, adding that his appointment “marks a pivotal chapter” in the airline’s ongoing transformation. It said that he had managed three airlines as CEO and was considered a “world expert” in transforming and reviving airlines, with over 30 years of experience. “As Hamilton-Manns assumes the role of CEO, the consortium and the entire management board extend their deepest gratitude to the outgoing CEO, Air Vice Marshal (AVM) Amir Hayat, for his outstanding service and dedication to this vital national role,” the statement said. It added that over his four-and-a-half-year tenure, Hayat’s leadership was “instrumental in navigating the airline through significant industry challenges”. “His relentless efforts were central to initiating comprehensive structural reforms, optimising operational efficiencies and successfully preparing the airline for its highly anticipated privatisation phase,” it said. “The foundation he has laid will be critical to the carrier’s future commercial viability and success,” it added. The statement said that with Hamilton-Manns at the helm, PIA was confident that his extensive industry expertise would accelerate strategic objectives, elevate service standards and drive sustainable profitability in this new era. According to Forbes Middle East , Hamilton-Manns was previously the CEO of Oman’s SalamAir and Kazakhstan-based FlyArystan. He also held roles at South African Airways and Virgin Australia. The national flag carrier was privatised in December last year through an auction. A consortium led by Arif Habib Corporation Limited had won the auction for 75 per cent shares of PIA in December last year, making a winning bid of Rs135 billion. The Arif Habib-led consortium, which took charge in June this year, had vowed to transform the loss-making airline through operational restructuring, fleet expansion, and improved customer service. On Sunday, the carrier’s first Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner , acquired on lease last month, arrived in Islamabad from London as flight PK786. A PIA spokesperson said that the carrier was the first Pakistani airline to have added a Boeing 787-9 to its fleet.

How War is Reshaping Iran’s “Axis of Resistance” eschelhaas Fri, 10/16/2026 - 18:13 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Iranians commute past a billboard depicting slain Lebanese Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah and Iran's slain supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in Tehran on September 27, 2026. ATTA KENARE / AFP Commentary / Middle East & North Africa 16 October 2026 12 minutes How War is Reshaping Iran’s “Axis of Resistance” Three years of hostilities have transformed Tehran’s network of allies in the Middle East. The Islamic Republic is now relying more heavily on itself, while adapting its relationships with partners whose diminished military utility has not necessarily reduced its commitment to their protection. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Hamidreza Azizi Senior Analyst, Iran https://x.com/HamidRezaAz Related Tags Iran Israel/Palestine Lebanon Syria Developments since 7 October 2023, when Hamas staged its deadly attacks on southern Israel, have transformed Iran’s network of state and non-state allies in the Middle East, as well as their role in Tehran’s military planning and deterrence posture. The weakening of Hamas and Hizbollah at Israel’s hands in the last three years, the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s regime in Syria in December 2024 and, above all, the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran launched in February have altered the vectors of Iranian influence. Together, these events have exposed the limits of an Iranian strategy that had relied chiefly on regional partners to deter adversaries and keep any armed confrontation away from Iran itself. Instead, Tehran now places greater weight on capabilities under its direct control: missiles, drones and the ability to obstruct traffic in the Strait of Hormuz. This evolution does not mean that the “ axis of resistance ”, as Iran calls its collection of allies, has lost all relevance. Rather, it means that axis members are now assuming different functions and that Tehran is approaching them differently. Yemen’s Houthis have gained particularly significant strategic value for Iran because their ability to threaten Red Sea shipping complements Tehran’s leverage over the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf. In Iraq, major Shiite factions also remain important political partners, even as Tehran increasingly turns to smaller armed groups to conduct military operations. Overall, the result is a more fragmented network in which heightened local autonomy among Iran’s non-state partners coexists with tighter Iranian control of select cells and smaller armed organisations. Nor is a weaker “axis of resistance” necessarily synonymous with diminished Iranian commitment to its partners. Hizbollah’s lesser contribution to Iranian deterrence, for example, has not reduced Tehran’s determination to protect the Lebanese Shiite movement. To the contrary, Iran has shown itself more willing to use force in Hizbollah’s defence; it also has conditioned reaching a deal terminating its hostilities with the United States on an end to Israel’s campaign in Lebanon. In other terms, Iran still may be drawn into conflicts on its regional partners’ behalf, even as they have become less capable of shielding it from attack. From the Levant to Maritime Chokepoints Prior to October 2023, Iran’s Middle East strategy centred on the Levant . Syria under Assad’s rule was the linchpin, the only Arab state allied with Iran, which provided it with substantial benefits: a land corridor linking Iran and its Iraqi Shiite partners to Hizbollah; proximity to Israel’s borders; and a logistical hub that enabled Tehran to project its influence to the eastern Mediterranean seaboard. In June 2024, Yahya Rahim Safavi , a former commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps who was then military adviser to Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, likened Iran’s reach through the axis to that of the ancient Persian empire under Cyrus and Xerxes. The advantages of alliance with Assad explain why, over a decade of civil war in Syria, Tehran defended his regime at significant cost. Hizbollah fighters also helped the regime a great deal, battling both its domestic opponents and ISIS. Hizbollah was useful in another important way, offering Tehran a means of threatening Israel from adjacent territory, thus ostensibly deterring it from direct strikes on Iran itself. If Assad’s Syria was a linchpin of the Islamic Republic’s Middle East strategy, the Shiite movement in Lebanon was a principal engine. [Assad’s fall] deprived Iran of its sole Arab state partner and disrupted its supply line to Hizbollah. This arrangement has suffered severe damage since October 2023 , when Hamas – apparently taking even Iran’s leadership by surprise – attacked Israel. The Gaza campaign that Israel launched in response dealt the axis a first blow, although Iran’s relationship with the Palestinian group has never been on par with those it has enjoyed with its other affiliates. Assad’s fall – indirectly part of the chain of events triggered by the Hamas attacks – was far more consequential. It deprived Iran of its sole Arab state partner and disrupted its supply line to Hizbollah. After Hizbollah entered the post-2023 fray, Israeli counter-attacks also inflicted substantial losses on the Lebanese movement’s leadership and military assets, while causing significant death, destruction and displacement in the country. As a result, other Lebanese factions began issuing more urgent calls on Hizbollah to disarm. The setbacks reinforced one another: rebuilding a degraded Hizbollah was a far more daunting task without the Syrian channel that had previously sustained it. These losses notwithstanding, Tehran has yet to forsake the Levant. Hizbollah still has a strong, institutionalised relationship with Iran, significant political weight in Lebanon and the capacity to regroup, at least in part. The Israeli incursions into southern Syria following the Assad regime’s demise may also have benefits for Iran. The Islamic Republic may be banking on local resistance to Israel eventually creating openings for renewed Iranian influence in Syria, though this prospect remains uncertain. For now, Iran has turned its attention to an arena closer to its borders where it retains heftier clout. On 8 June, Esmail Qaani , commander ofthe Revolutionary Guards’ overseas operations arm, the Qods Force, described an emerging “security belt” stretching from the Gulf to the Red Sea. When compared to Safavi’s formulation two years prior, the phrase captures a shift in emphasis from the Levant to the maritime routes linking the Gulf to the western Indian Ocean, a theatre in which Iran’s sway comes more directly from its own place on the map. The Islamic Republic requires neither an allied state nor a non-state partner to project power in the Strait of Hormuz; it can station missiles and drones nearby or even deep inland to threaten naval or commercial vessels in these waters. Tehran’s influence over maritime routes upon which states near and far depend for trade in oil, gas and other vital commodities is boosted by its partnership with the Houthis, who can fire at ships passing in either direction through the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab. Though it no longer serves as a land bridge for arms transfers to Syria and Lebanon, Iraq nonetheless plays an important part in this changing landscape. In particular, it is a locus for coordination between the Houthis and Iraqi armed groups , as well as between the Qods Force and Iraqi groups that have conducted attacks on Gulf Arab states. A More Fragmented Network The shift in Iran’s primary focus from the Levant to the seas has gone hand in hand with organisational changes. Under its late commander Qassem Soleimani, the Qods Force was the principal coordinator of “axis of resistance” activities. Since the U.S. killed Soleimani in January 2020, the Qods Force has not played the same role. Subsequent wars and leadership losses, both within the Revolutionary Guards and among its partners, further discombobulated command structures and impaired joint military operations. As a result, Iran has had to adapt its relationships with groups whose military capabilities and domestic constraints themselves have changed. It has increasingly been compelled to work through smaller groups or selected elements of established organisations. This trend has been most evident in Iraq. As the years passed after Saddam Hussein’s ouster, older Shiite political movements acquired key government positions and economic interests, thus becoming more beholden to popular constituencies. As a result, they are now more hesitant to engage in military action that risks provoking retaliation or eroding their standing. This reluctance was apparent early in the present U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, when several major Iraqi Shiite armed groups declined to mobilise on Tehran’s behalf. Iran had to rely on smaller, less prominent ones – drawn from the self-styled Islamic Resistance in Iraq – to come to its aid. Iraqi sources speak of a network of clandestine cells established by the Revolutionary Guards and operating outside established militias’ command structures that reportedly has been responsible for attacks on Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. These nimbler, smaller groups offer Tehran several advantages. They require fewer resources, they can conceal their affiliations and they can ignore the political constraints holding back their larger counterparts. Their greater ideological cohesion also arguably makes them easier for Tehran to direct. More institutionalised Iraqi Shiite groups remain important to Tehran, notwithstanding their reticence regarding military action in Iran’s defence. But their role has shifted: they are useful principally because they help Iran preserve influence in the country as well as the political space in which smaller armed groups are free to operate. Iran’s changing relationship with Hizbollah illustrates another type of adjustment to similar pressures. Though the movement retains a substantial organisation that helps Tehran sustain influence in Lebanon, Hizbollah’s military actions increasingly resemble those of a guerrilla group – quick-hitting raids that leave the group less vulnerable to Israeli airstrikes and intelligence penetration. Its use of first-person-view drones – drones using a live video feed from an onboard camera – to attack Israeli forces in southern Lebanon showcased the effectiveness of inexpensive technology, even as the movement has lost its more sophisticated capabilities. An Iranian expert with ties to both the Revolutionary Guards and Hizbollah told Crisis Group that Qods Force commanders have been directly involved in this revamping, including efforts to work through smaller units and help Hizbollah fighters adopt more agile tactics. Deterrence Moves Closer to Home, but the Axis Remains Important These changes reflect a broader reassessment of Iran’s deterrence posture. Its earlier approach heavily relied on the concept of “ forward defence ” ensured by regional partners, supplemented by the threat of direct retaliation from its own territory. The “axis of resistance” gave the Islamic Republic strategic depth , discouraging its adversaries from attacking it and keeping conflict distant from its borders. Only if that first layer of protection were to fail were Iranian missiles and drones to be used to shoot back. The past three years of war have starkly exposed the limits inherent in this arrangement. Iran’s regional network did not prevent direct attacks on the country – whether the major exchanges with Israel in 2024, the surprise Israeli attack in June 2025 or the more substantial confrontation with the U.S. and Israel beginning in February. As the deterrence value of axis partners dropped, Tehran was compelled to place greater weight on its own capabilities: missiles, drones and geographical leverage. If military setbacks have transformed the role played by the axis, they have not eliminated its utility to Iran. Yet, if military setbacks have transformed the role played by the axis, they have not eliminated its utility to Iran. Though the axis as a whole no longer serves as the primary foundation of Iran’s deterrence, decision-makers in Tehran believe that certain partners can play important roles in particular circumstances as they magnify Iran’s own capabilities and geographical leverage. Their experience during the present conflict with the U.S. has only bolstered this conviction. The Houthis have attained particular importance in the Islamic Republic’s thinking, which helps explain reports that Tehran has provided them with both guidance and military assistance. Tehran’s efforts in July to establish direct flights to Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen illustrated the multidimensional nature of this support: the flights both challenged restrictions imposed by Yemen’s internationally recognised government and Saudi Arabia on Houthi rule and reportedly carried Revolutionary Guards commanders, military advisers and missile- and drone-related equipment. Hizbollah, too, has retained its usefulness for Tehran. The movement attacked Israel following February’s U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran, forcing Israel to contend with an additional front and placing further demands on its air defences. True, that supporting role was a far cry from the crucial deterrent function the movement was intended to play, a reflection of its diminished capabilities. Iranian officials have nevertheless continued to frame their confrontation with the U.S. and Israel as extending to Iran’s Middle East partners, Hizbollah in particular. In June, in a remarkable role reversal, Iran launched missiles at Israel in response to its campaign against Hizbollah, thereby marshalling its own forces in defence of its partner rather than the other way around. Moreover, it conditioned its acceptance of the (short-lived) 17 June memorandum of understanding halting hostilities with the U.S. on cessation of Israeli attacks in Lebanon: the opening clause explicitly included Lebanon in the ceasefire and affirmed Lebanese sovereignty and territorial integrity. Israel persisted with its offensive, however, including at Ali al-Taher , a strategic Hizbollah position in southern Lebanon where Israel besieged (and, in mid-September, demolished) an underground command and weapons complex. To Iranian officials, who had reportedly sent warnings that any such act would provoke a “forceful” response, the demolition was a reminder that Iranian threats of renewed missile attacks were an insufficient deterrent. Still, Iran’s stance showcased its commitment to axis members whose military utility has faded but not been erased. Decades of institutional ties, ideological affinity and investment help explain Iran’s approach. Decades of institutional ties, ideological affinity and investment help explain Iran’s approach. According to Iranian experts interviewed by Crisis Group, several members of the security establishment regard Hizbollah’s survival in particular as being closely tied to Iran’s own security, giving the relationship a significance that extends beyond the movement’s immediate military capabilities. This outlook has surfaced in public debates. In a January 2025 interview published by Iran’s Strategic Council on Foreign Relations, former diplomat Hadi Seyyed Afghahi argued that pressure on militant groups in Iraq, Lebanon and Yemen was aimed at “Iran and, more generally, the Shiites of the region”. Therefore, Tehran could not remain indifferent to these groups’ fate. Likewise, in December 2025, Ali Samadzadeh , an analyst with close ties to the regime, argued that Iran should be prepared to intervene militarily if Israel attacked Hizbollah, describing an assault on Lebanon as a prelude to renewed war with Iran. Defending regional partners, in this view, is part and parcel of protecting Iran itself. In short, where Tehran regards a partner as key to its own security, the fact that the partner has been weakened arguably – and perhaps paradoxically – provides Iran with added reason to intervene on its behalf. Efforts to curb Iranian influence by targeting allied groups may therefore draw Tehran into conflicts – a marked departure from the role these groups once played in shielding the Islamic Republic from direct involvement in hostilities. The extent of Iranian involvement is likely to depend on the particular relationship in question and the risks and costs inherent in intervention. But the bottom line is that its partners’ diminished military capabilities will not necessarily reduce Iran’s exposure to, or participation in, their respective conflicts. A Shifting Picture After three years of hostilities involving Iran’s partners and, since February, Iran itself, the “axis of resistance” is neither down nor out, but it is not what it once was, either in the function it serves or in Tehran’s relationship to its various members. The changes have been manifold. First, some of its members’ military capabilities have been significantly degraded. Secondly, direct confrontation with the U.S. and Israel has revealed the groups’ limited deterrent value and their inability to keep conflict away from Iranian territory. Finally, and partly as a result of their lessened status, they have come under growing domestic political, economic and security pressure, hindering their ability to directly participate in confrontations involving the Islamic Republic. These changes do not rule out these groups’ continued close operational ties to Tehran; nor do they mean an end to Iran’s commitment to their protection. But, together, they constrain the groups’ freedom of action. As a result, the focus of the Islamic Republic’s strategic doctrine has pivoted from allied non-state actors toward its own capabilities. This adjustment undoubtedly has preserved Iran’s ability to project power in its neighbourhood. But it does not come without serious risk, insofar as it has led Tehran to more directly bear the costs and dangers of confrontation. The Islamic Republic may well find ways to manage the consequences of its partners’ weakened clout by coming to their aid when they are endangered, giving them breathing space to regroup and using its own military assets to deter its foes, including by ensuring that others – notably Gulf Arab states – suffer the consequences of Middle East war. In so doing, Iran hopes to discourage future attacks. But this approach also risks deepening hostility among its neighbours, potentially encouraging closer security cooperation among Iran’s adversaries and heightening the very pressures Tehran seeks to reduce. Two main blocs, of nearly equal weight according to polls, face off against each other: an alliance of hard-right parties dominated by Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister and head of the Likud party, and an opposing camp led by Gadi Eisenkot, a former army chief of staff and head of Yashar, a centre-right party he founded last year. The Dilemmas Facing Palestinian Citizens in Israel’s Elections mloukili Thu, 10/22/2026 - 16:47 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Op-Ed / Middle East & North Africa 22 October 2026 7 minutes The Dilemmas Facing Palestinian Citizens in Israel’s Elections Originally published in ISPI Arab-led parties could hold the balance of power in Israel's election. But as Palestinian citizens seek safety and equal rights, rival strategies and rejection by Jewish opposition leaders threaten to turn electoral leverage into political exclusion. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Amjad Iraqi Senior Analyst, Israel/Palestine https://x.com/aj_iraqi Related Tags Israel/Palestine In Arab towns and cities across Israel, streets and buildings are lined with posters and billboards about the upcoming national elections on 27 October. Two slates representing Palestinian citizens of Israel – a tri-party alliance called the Joint List (made up of Hadash, Ta’al and Balad) and the United Arab List, also known as Ra’am – are competing for the community’s votes, which, according to polls, could give the parties a combined total of 13 to 15 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. Many Palestinian citizens would agree that this election may be one of the most consequential in recent memory. But depending on who you ask, the principal contenders for their ballots appear either strikingly different or strangely similar. Despite an expanding matrix of laws and policies rendering them second-class citizens, Palestinians in Israel have long used their right to vote to assert their voice in the Knesset and to procure State resources to meet their socioeconomic needs. This year, fear has been a major driving motive . The far-right government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has waged a relentless campaign against Palestinians – from the devastating war in Gaza, to heightened settler violence and accelerated annexation in the West Bank, to greater repression and discrimination inside Israel. Under the Ministry of National Security headed by Itamar Ben-Gvir, Israel’s police have condoned, even more so than in the past, the organised crime and gun violence that have mushroomed in Arab localities, making personal security the top priority for most Arab voters. In theory, the Palestinian community – which makes up a fifth of Israel’s citizenry and about 17% of eligible voters – has some leverage to alter this state of affairs. Its clout derives not just from sheer numbers but from the fractured nature of Israel’s political landscape. Polls consistently show that neither Netanyahu’s ruling coalition nor the Jewish opposition led by Yashar! leader Gadi Eisenkot can secure a parliamentary majority on their own. Projections give the Joint List eight to nine seats and Ra’am five to six seats, with commentators describing the parties as potential “kingmakers” . Yet the projections tell only part of the story of a deeper schism at the heart of Palestinian politics in Israel and of the dilemmas that Arab voters face as they try to protect their rights – and indeed, their very presence – in the heart of an increasingly aggressive Israeli State. Unwanted Partners Given the likely shortfall in the Knesset, logic would dictate that the anti-Netanyahu bloc should partner with the Arab parties to oust the long-time prime minister and his far-right allies such as Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich. Yet political prejudices are outweighing electoral mathematics . Almost all the Jewish opposition parties insist that they will not ally themselves with their Arab counterparts , with some even refusing to accept them as external backers of a minority government. Some, like Yisrael Beiteinu leader Avigdor Lieberman, are open about their hostility towards Palestinian citizens, and some, like Together leader Naftali Bennett, worry about discouraging Jewish voters still reeling from Hamas’s 7 October 2023 attacks. Other still, such as Yesh Atid leader Yair Lapid, are reluctant to be constrained by the demands of Arab parties. Eisenkot himself has said that he is seeking to build a “Zionist majority” coalition and that none of the Arab lists meets his criteria for partnership, such as supporting mandatory national service in the army or in civilian bodies (towards which Palestinian citizens are largely hostile), recognising Israel as a “Jewish and democratic” State (thereby accepting its ethno-nationalist character) and labelling Hamas a terrorist organisation. Split Responses Shunned and delegitimised as they are, the Joint List and Ra’am still insist they are prepared to play a part in deciding the next Israeli government. They have few illusions about an Eisenkot-led coalition, whose leaders echo many of Netanyahu’s right-wing views. Nonetheless, both Arab slates strongly believe that a renewed mandate for the far-right could amount to an existential threat to the community, let alone to Palestinians in the occupied territories. They argue that it is incumbent upon them to prevent Netanyahu’s return by any political means at their disposal. As one Arab parliamentarian put it to the International Crisis Group (ICG), “Our goal is to slow the bleeding – and I don’t mean that metaphorically”. While recognising the common danger, the two slates are at odds over how to wield their leverage . According to Joint List leader Yousef Jabareen , the tri-party alliance is ready to provide a “safety net” for an Israeli minority government as external backers in Parliament if the government pledges to tackle organised crime, halt punitive home demolitions and open a diplomatic pathway towards a Palestinian State. This offer has its antecedents: in the 1990s, Arab parties gave former prime minister Yitzhak Rabin external parliamentary support in the context of the Oslo Accords, and in 2019 and 2020, the Joint List offered its backing to Blue and White leader Benny Gantz to eject Netanyahu (which Gantz rejected). For Ra’am leader Mansour Abbas , though, any demands that relate to the occupation are likely to hinder cooperation with Jewish parties, which have grown more hawkish on the Palestinian question, at the expense of advancing the Arab community’s pressing needs. While in principle supportive of Palestinian rights and statehood, Ra’am has campaigned almost exclusively on the pledges of fighting crime and securing fresh budgets, even allying himself with former police commander and Jewish politician Yoav Segalovitz to signal that focus. Abbas, who made Ra’am a partner in the 2021-22 Bennett-Lapid government, argues that when it comes to decision making, “Either you are at the table, or you are left to the side”. Murky Prospects Experts generally agree that Palestinian citizens’ turnout at the ballot is likely to be high, with some estimating it could reach about 60-65% of eligible Arab voters. But many of those voters feel torn between two rival slates that may have little hope of acquiring the influence they claim is within their reach. If Eisenkot expects to be prime minister, he would have to either swallow his antagonism towards the Arab parties or partner with members of the rival bloc, perhaps even Netanyahu’s Likud. When faced with the same choice in 2020 after two inconclusive election rounds, Gantz opted to ally with Netanyahu. Though Eisenkot insists he will not do the same, it remains to be seen whether numerical necessity will press him toward a national unity government with Likud. Recent weeks have only deepened the murkiness. In September, with overwhelming endorsement from both coalition and opposition members, the Knesset’s Central Elections Committee disqualified the two Arab slates and two Arab politicians from running in the election. The Supreme Court overturned most of the decisions, but it supported the disqualification of Balad leader Sami Abu Shehadeh over an article he had written describing the 7 October attacks as an “important historic event” and compelled him to either quit the race or receive a more consequential legal ruling; ultimately, he chose to bow out. Regardless of the court’s other rulings, the near-unanimous disdain towards the Arab parties delivered a chilling message that tolerance for Palestinians in the Knesset was wearing thin and that more political attacks on their representatives were likely in store. Internal disputes are also souring Arab voters. Some have been frustrated by the Joint List’s squabbles over how to allocate seats among its three parties, by a public saga over a now-ejected Hadash politician accused of sexual harassment and by disputes over the handling of Abu Shehadeh’s disqualification case. Meanwhile, some blame Ra’am for refusing to learn from the limitations it faced under the Bennett-Lapid government (such as when Ra’am members refused to join the coalition in passing a law that enshrined Israel’s ban on Palestinian family unification), for unduly taking credit for budgets secured by the Joint List in prior years, and for ignoring Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank at a time when they are being subjected to horrendous violence and suffering. Tensions Between Strategies With so much at stake, Palestinian citizens are desperate for a breakthrough in the coming elections. For some, Ra’am arguably offers the more pragmatic way forward. “The modern Arab voter is not interested in the old slogans” promoted by Arab parties, one political analyst told the International Crisis Group. Some Joint List supporters privately confess that Abbas is making a strong and coherent case for his approach. Several have even questioned the Joint List’s claim that its strategy is fundamentally different from Ra’am’s , further arguing that Ra’am’s focus on domestic issues could persuade the opposition to include it in a governing coalition and, in exchange for its support, agree to provide resources to address crime and violence – or at a minimum keep the far-right out of power. Still, Ra’am’s near-term pragmatism stands in tension with the Joint List’s long-term warning that Israel’s military rule over Palestinians beyond the Green Line cannot be detached from the shrinking rights of Palestinians inside the line. With Israel’s political spectrum sliding further rightwards, Arab parties have been among the only voices inside Israel reminding the country that the occupation is an existential problem . Ejecting the far-right could help reduce the speed and severity of Israel’s policies, but Netanyahu’s successors may prove to be almost as determined to preserve Israeli supremacy. As such, few Palestinian citizens believe that this election can bring about seismic changes. Their priorities are instead to mitigate Israel’s harms and restore some semblance of safety . The Arab parties are promising that they can advance these goals by clinching a large share of Knesset seats. Yet their voters will need other factors to make their voices count: a Jewish-Israeli politics that respects non-Jews as equals, a revitalised Palestinian leadership to guide the wider, broken national movement and a mix of international pressure and engagement to turn the conflict towards more constructive paths. REUTERS / Adnan Abidi Report 360 / Asia-Pacific 23 October 2026 20+ minutes A Trigger in Jammu and Kashmir: Militant Violence under Indian Central Rule In 2019, India made far-reaching changes to governance in Jammu and Kashmir, with the aim of quelling insurgency. Its policy has succeeded in some ways, but backfired in others. New Delhi will need to shift tack if it hopes to bring peace to the region. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print "> Download PDF Related Tags India Pakistan What’s new? Seven years after New Delhi revoked Jammu and Kashmir’s semi-autonomous status, ostensibly to curb militant activity and bring peace in its stead, disaffection is festering among Kashmiri Muslims. Militant groups are evolving in both their tactics and their chosen targets. Why does it matter? New Delhi’s tough security approach in the region has sparked a militant response. A deadly terrorist attack in April 2025 triggered clashes between India and Pakistan that ended in a stalemate. Another incident in Indian-administered Kashmir or elsewhere in India could once again trigger conflict between the two nuclear powers. What should be done? New Delhi should push forward plans to restore Jammu and Kashmir’s statehood, hand powers back to regional authorities and rein in its harsh, counterproductive use of anti-terror laws. India and Pakistan, with the support of foreign governments, should seek to revive high-level back channels to prevent a future confrontation. Executive Summary Seven years after India revoked Jammu and Kashmir’s semi-autonomous status and ushered in sweeping reforms, ostensibly to bring peace to the Himalayan region, bitterness festers.
