Kashmiri militants, whether local or foreign, could well aim to conduct another terror attack on Indian soil. 127 The U.S. Directorate of National Intelligence assessed in its 2026 report that “conditions exist for terrorist actors to continue to create catalysts for crises”. See “Annual Threat Assessment of the US Intelligence Community”, Office of the Director of National Intelligence, March 2026, p. 24. For some observers, the next India-Pakistan conflict is thus “a question of when, not if”. 128 “In West Asia, a widening conflict with no clear ends”, Hindustan Times , 7 March 2026; “The faint hope for peace between India and Pakistan”, Time , 26 June 2026. It is true that, despite its combative posture and promises to retaliate against all attacks, the Indian government has proven more cautious than expected, taking great care not to blame Pakistan after the November 2025 New Delhi blast. But whether it can withstand domestic pressure in the event of another large-scale attack is hard to predict. In these circumstances, resuming a modicum of dialogue with Islamabad has taken on extra urgency. Insisting that Pakistan still backs anti-India jihadists, India has ... turned down Islamabad’s proposal of back-channel talks. New Delhi has thus far rebuffed Pakistan’s diplomatic overtures, including the Pakistani prime minister’s offer of dialogue to settle contentious issues, from terrorism to disputes over water sharing and the fate of Jammu and Kashmir. 129 Crisis Group Briefing, India-Pakistan: Avoiding a War in Waiting , op. cit. See also “PM urges India to ‘hold’ meaningful dialogue on Kashmir”, The News , 5 February 2025. Insisting that Pakistan still backs anti-India jihadists, India has also turned down Islamabad’s proposal of back-channel talks. 130 Maleeha Lodhi, “A year on, stalemate persists”, Dawn , 15 June 2026. The two sides have reportedly participated in a few discreet Track 1.5 and 2 dialogues, unofficial discussions held by former officials and experts who are not representatives of any state. 131 “India Pakistan held Track 1.5, 2 meetings after Operation Sindoor”, Hindustan Times , 17 April 2026. As a former senior Pakistani diplomat noted, however, such exchanges have limited value since participants seldom deviate from the stated positions of their home countries. 132 Lodhi, “A year on, stalemate persists”, op. cit. Signs of greater inclination to engage with Islamabad have nevertheless begun to emerge on the Indian side. A senior leader from the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), the BJP’s powerful parent organisation, has for the first time spoken up about the need to engage with Pakistan, arguing that while India has every right to “respond appropriately” to terror incidents backed by Islamabad, it should leave the door to dialogue open. 133 “Why has the RSS called for dialogue with Pakistan?”, The Hindu , 17 May 2026; “‘India should not close doors for dialogue with Pakistan’: RSS general secretary Dattatreya Hosabale”, Times of India , 12 May 2026. Given the RSS’s influence, this stance could help assuage public hostility to diplomacy with Pakistan. 134 The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (the National Volunteers Association, or RSS) is a Hindu nationalist organisation founded in 1925, of which the BJP is just one of many wings. With millions of members, it is considered the largest NGO in the world. For a critical view of the RSS, see “Mamdani opposes NYC event with leader of India’s Hindu nationalist group”, Reuters, 26 August 2026. Islamabad has reacted cautiously to the RSS call, with the foreign ministry waiting to see if its views reflect India’s official policy. 135 “FO waiting to see how India reacts to ‘pro-dialogue chorus”, Dawn , 15 May 2026. Few in Pakistan, however, are optimistic regarding the revival of formal talks with India so long as the BJP government continues to accuse the country of supporting jihadist groups and fighting a proxy war with its neighbour. 136 Crisis Group telephone interviews, August 2026. See also Touqir Hussain, “Modi’s Pakistan policy”, Dawn , 13 August 2026. Hussain is a former Pakistan ambassador. The absence of direct lines of communication beyond military-to-military channels increases conflict risks, including as the result of miscalculation or misunderstanding. Despite abiding distrust of its neighbour, India has, in the past, maintained communication through back channels with Pakistan, even in times of crisis. 137 The prime ministers of India and Pakistan spoke to each other even at the height of the Kargil conflict of 1999, for example, and the two national security advisers have been in regular touch during other tense episodes. At present, however, the only communication channel in place is a hotline between the directors general of military operations. Crisis Group Briefing, India-Pakistan: Avoiding a War in Waiting , op. cit. See also “India and Pakistan: Neighbours who do not talk to each other”, The India Forum , 10 April 2026. Since there are few prospects for formal talks between India and Pakistan’s top leaders, behind-the-scenes diplomacy could play a vital role in defusing the threat of fresh clashes. Such quiet contacts could enable political leaders to communicate, if not directly, then at least through their national security advisers. 138 Crisis Group Briefing, India-Pakistan: Avoiding a War in Waiting , op. cit. Reviving such a mechanism would allow both sides to communicate their red lines and, perhaps most importantly, avoid misunderstanding or misinterpretation of the other’s actions. They should establish this bilateral channel outside the limelight to avoid the domestic pressures both might face should news of it leak. At the same time, Indian authorities could make it clear to the public that any level of engagement would not amount to normalising relations or offering concessions to Islamabad, including over its territorial claims on Kashmir. Authorities in Islamabad could also assure the Pakistani public that Pakistan’s position on Kashmir’s disputed status or other contentious issues such as the country’s rights under the Indus Waters Treaty would not be compromised. Resuming quiet diplomacy would allow both [India and Pakistan] to share, examine and discuss their respective allegations outside the public eye. Even then, back-channel diplomacy is unlikely to make much headway if the Indian and Pakistani governments succumb to the temptation of nationalist outbursts and tit-for-tat allegations against each other. A tentative diplomatic opening is also likely to fail if Pakistan does not address India’s suspicions of continued support for anti-India jihadist groups more robustly. It is in Islamabad’s interest to rigorously enforce the law banning all jihadist entities. In return, Islamabad will expect New Delhi to respond to its concerns about alleged Indian backing for anti-Pakistan Baloch militant groups and the Pakistani Taliban. Progress in reducing mutual trust on such contentious issues is unlikely to happen overnight. But a high-level back channel between the national security advisers could still play an important role in this respect. Resuming quiet diplomacy would allow both to share, examine and discuss their respective allegations outside the public eye. Foreign governments that enjoy friendly relations with both parties, such as the U.S., the UK, EU member states, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and other Gulf countries, can also help stabilise the relationship. Considering India’s sensitivities regarding foreign interference or mediation on the Kashmir issue, external powers should move cautiously with quiet, behind-the-scenes diplomacy. They should emphasise that it is in New Delhi and Islamabad’s mutual interest to ensure a sustainable peace in South Asia, encouraging them to use high-level back channels to defuse potential conflict triggers. After seven years, the tough security measures and federal rule have not only failed to bring peace but may also have fostered support for militant groups in some circles. Srinagar, Kashmir, India. November 2025. CRISIS GROUP / Praveen Donthi VI. Conclusion Seven years after the Indian government revoked Jammu and Kashmir’s special autonomous status, redrew its boundaries, overhauled its administrative set-up and undertook numerous reforms ostensibly to foster peace, the threats to local and regional security from the restive Himalayan region persist – and have arguably grown more serious given their impact on relations with Pakistan. Though the government has succeeded in reducing conflict-related violence, the stringent measures it has employed to do so and the threat it has posed to Kashmiris’ sense of identity are fuelling deep discontent. New Delhi’s efforts to impose central rule appear not to have achieved their goal of eradicating militancy. They may even have fostered support in some circles for insurgent groups. If it is to achieve a durable peace in Jammu and Kashmir, India should address as a priority Kashmiris’ growing disaffection. Ideally, that would start by honouring the promise to restore the region’s statehood, paving the way to reinstatement of a democratically elected regional government with real power. New Delhi should also review its tactics in combating militant groups, particularly by being more discriminating in the way it applies its anti-terror laws. Sparked by a terrorist attack in Indian-administered Kashmir, the brief but intense clashes between India and Pakistan in 2025 were a stark reminder of how devastating this oft-forgotten dispute could be if it gets out of hand. Resumption of some form of dialogue between the two nuclear neighbours is essential, preferably through a discreet back channel. With its aspirations for a “New Kashmir” proving overly optimistic, the Indian government should do more to ensure that this unresolved conflict does not become the trigger for far greater harm. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print 23 October 2026 CUBA The UN General Assembly will vote next week on its annual resolution condemning the U.S. embargo on Cuba, in place for more than six decades. Last year’s resolution passed 165-7. Washington is seeking to reduce the resolution’s backing as the Trump administration pursues a broader economic pressure campaign on the island (including restrictions on oil shipments and new secondary sanctions). U.S. Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz hosted an event featuring Cuban dissidents, who argued that supporting the resolution excuses the Cuban government’s human rights abuses while obscuring its role in the country’s economic crisis. Cuban diplomats denounced the panel as an attempt to deflect attention from the embargo’s effects. Crisis Group expert Michael Bustamante says the confrontation illustrates the unfortunate either-or terms in which the debate is often framed. Decrying the humanitarian consequences of U.S. measures need not mean absolving the Cuban government of responsibility for its economic policy failures or its suppression of dissent. STRAIT OF HORMUZ October has already seen Iran hit more ships in or around the Strait of Hormuz than any previous month of the war that the U.S. and Israel launched in February. Tehran’s escalation comes after the volume of crude oil moving through the strait reached pre-war levels, largely through a scheme by which a few risk-tolerant tankers are assuming the danger of hauling barrels through the waterway before transferring their cargo to more risk-averse vessels outside it. Crisis Group expert Chris Newton says the question now is whether Iran can make these “shuttle runs” too costly. If it cannot, it will lose leverage in any negotiations with the U.S. and Gulf Arab countries that may transpire. But if it can, its attacks could prompt retaliatory U.S. strikes. U.S. - UKRAINE Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced on Tuesday that U.S. intelligence sharing, crucial for advance warning of incoming Russian ballistic missiles, had been restored. At the same time, there were conflicting reports on a slowdown in Ukraine’s access to the Starlink satellite system, which it depends on for battlefield communications and defensive drones. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the “throttling” of Starlink, which is run by billionaire Elon Musk's company SpaceX, was a technical error that “no one ordered”. The incident nonetheless fuelled speculation that the Trump administration is scaling back intelligence and technological support for Ukraine to strong-arm Kyiv into making concessions to Moscow ahead of the 3 November U.S. midterm elections. Wednesday’s meeting between Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff and Russian President Vladimir Putin, in which Witkoff called Putin a “humanitarian”, has done the same. Crisis Group expert Lucian Kim says Zelenskyy’s resistance to U.S. pressure has boosted his approval ratings at home. Polls show that a majority of Ukrainians oppose ceding territory in return for a peace settlement. 16 October 2026 IRAN Iranian attacks on shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz have surged in October to date, with more than two dozen vessels struck since the month began. Meanwhile, Washington is maintaining its blockade of Iranian ports while backing oil shipments along the Omani coast, where smaller tankers transfer cargo to larger vessels outside the strait. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says the uptick in Iranian strikes is an effort to counter a rebound in oil flows that showed Tehran’s grip on the Strait of Hormuz was weakening. Iran wants Washington to accept its proposed terms for a ceasefire that reopens the waterway in exchange for sanctions relief and an end to the U.S. blockade. But a diplomatic breakthrough appears less likely than the two sides setting off another escalatory spiral. SUDAN The Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, a UN-backed hunger monitor, warned Monday of growing famine risks in Sudan’s Darfur and Kordofan regions, driven by conflict, displacement and inadequate aid funding, and compounded by an El Niño-induced drought. This news comes as Sudan’s army reports advances against the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in parts of North Kordofan and West Darfur. Meanwhile, the RSF continues to mount attacks in Blue Nile and to target El Obeid in North Kordofan with drones. Crisis Group expert Shewit Woldemichael says the army’s gains could make it more confident of victory, while continued RSF offensives suggest that this group, too, sees opportunities for battlefield gains. The continued fighting is likely to further complicate diplomatic efforts to end the war and ease Sudan’s humanitarian crisis. UKRAINE This past Sunday, U.S. President Donald Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine, saying each had agreed to halt attacks on the other’s energy infrastructure, following a deal he made to buy Russian diesel and ease related U.S. sanctions. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he learned of the ceasefire through social media, adding that Washington threatened to suspend intelligence sharing unless Ukraine stopped striking Russian refineries. Ukrainian forces also reported restrictions on Starshield, the military version of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite service, which they depend on for communications and drone operations. Washington says it continues to share intelligence with Ukraine. Zelenskyy this week announced the resumption of refinery attacks as Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure continued unabated. Crisis Group expert Lucian Kim says any disruption to intelligence or communications would compound Ukraine’s difficulties in protecting its cities and power grid as winter approaches, leaving civilians more vulnerable to prolonged heating and electricity outages. 9 October 2026 HAITI Haiti’s electoral council announced changes to the country’s voting rules Tuesday. The new law, which will likely result in delays to polls presently scheduled for 13 December, will remove provisions that would have disqualified individuals subject to bilateral sanctions imposed by third countries from running for office. Those subject to UN sanctions remain barred from candidacy. The move comes as the UN Panel of Experts on Haiti, which makes private recommendations to the Security Council regarding who should be sanctioned, denounced several high-profile politicians for using gangs to fuel violence. Some UN Security Council members worry that sanctioning public figures could interfere with Haiti’s political process. Crisis Group expert Diego Da Rin says the risk of inaction is greater, however: those who have collaborated with gangs could return to power, further delaying resolution of the Haitian conflict. MALI On Tuesday, the Malian army recaptured Kidal, a strategically important city in the country’s north that had been held by the separatist Front for the Liberation of Azawad (FLA) since April. The FLA said it had decided to temporarily withdraw from Kidal as the army, backed by Russian Africa Corps paramilitaries, launched a large-scale offensive. Crisis Group expert Ibrahim Maïga says the recapture of Kidal is a significant military development. But without a political process to build on these gains, the takeover alone is unlikely to bring this conflict closer to a lasting resolution. UKRAINE A Russian attack on Kramatorsk in Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region killed at least 33 people on a public bus Thursday. Previous Russian strikes across the country Wednesday killed at least 28 others, including 22 when a missile hit a residential building. Kramatorsk – one of the cities Russia has been unable to capture in Donetsk – has become an important supply hub for the Ukrainian army. The attack came as Kyiv struck a data centre belonging to Russia’s largest technology company, Yandex, in the central Ryazan region, south east of Moscow. Crisis Group expert Lucian Kim says both sides are using long-range strikes to put pressure on their adversaries, though Russia’s aerial campaign is far more devastating, raising the number of casualties among the civilian population and upending daily life for millions. 2 October 2026 MYANMAR Military airstrikes on a market in Kyauktaw, Rakhine State, on Monday reportedly killed at least 50 people. The UN described the attack as one of the deadliest in the state since the 2021 coup. The Arakan Army, an ethnic Rakhine group, vowed on Tuesday to take “retaliatory measures” against those responsible. The strikes came amid a military counter-offensive launched in early September on several fronts in and around Rakhine to retake territory from the Arakan Army. It has made little headway, says Crisis Group expert Thomas Kean. The market raid was likely intended to punish civilians and disrupt trade and governance in Arakan Army-held areas of Rakhine. U.S. - IRAN U.S. and Iranian negotiators held indirect talks on the UN General Assembly’s sidelines to end a conflict now in its eighth month. On 26 September, U.S. President Donald Trump said he had rejected an Iranian ceasefire proposal but continued to make counteroffers. On Wednesday, Trump warned of further military action, saying: “We blow them up or make a deal”. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says prospects for a breakthrough appear slim: Tehran proposes reopening the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for the U.S. lifting its blockade of Iranian ports and releasing Iranian assets. Washington believes it has overcome Iran’s efforts to restrict shipping while continuing to weaken the Iranian economy. Tehran also wants to defer nuclear issues to subsequent talks; Washington seeks concessions up front. Fear of escalation could keep the door to engagement open, but significant gaps over substance and sequencing remain. YEMEN Fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and their allies intensified this week, including around Taiz, a city in the middle of the country, where the rebels have been seeking to cut the road link with Aden on the southern coast. Taiz is home to more than 2 million people, many of whom have been displaced from other parts of Yemen. Meanwhile, the World Health Organization warned that Yemen’s health system was nearing “breaking point” amid mounting casualties. Crisis Group expert Ahmed Nagi says Houthi success around Taiz could help consolidate the group’s gains along the Red Sea coast. Diplomacy faces substantial obstacles: the Houthis are unlikely to accept de-escalation without tangible concessions from Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s government, while Riyadh may seek limited battlefield gains before mediation. 25 September 2026 SOUTH SUDAN President Salva Kiir dissolved South Sudan’s transitional unity government Tuesday, three months before elections scheduled for 22 December, dismantling key power-sharing institutions established under the 2018 peace agreement. Following a hurriedly passed amendment to the National Elections Act, Kiir dismissed all five vice presidents, including his long-time rival First Vice President Riek Machar, and installed a caretaker government composed entirely of loyalists. Crisis Group expert Daniel Akech says the changes allow Kiir to concentrate authority in his hands. Greater control of state institutions could help him retain power, through either a stage-managed election or a delay that prolongs his administration. The resulting political exclusion risks provoking greater conflict in an already deeply fractured country. UNITED NATIONS World leaders met this week in New York for the UN General Assembly’s annual high-level session. Crisis Group expert Daniel Forti says the week’s events proved that states still value the UN as a forum for discussing global concerns, even if common ground between them remains elusive. Some countries expect the next Secretary-General to single-handedly get the UN back on track and provide solutions for crises around the world. That attitude is short-sighted. The UN needs the conviction of its members to tackle global risks from deadly conflict to artificial intelligence. Whether states choose to work together – or continue down the path of international fragmentation – will determine whether the next decade at the UN is defined by diplomacy or disorder. U.S. - CHINA President Donald Trump hosted Chinese leader Xi Jinping for a state visit in Washington this week. Xi touted their personal rapport, called for “healthy” bilateral competition “within bounds” and argued that U.S.-China cooperation is needed to address most global challenges. Crisis Group expert Ali Wyne says the summit’s outcome was modest: the two leaders agreed to extend by two months the trade truce that they blessed in Busan, South Korea last October; it was due to expire on 10 November. They do not appear to have made a breakthrough on managing cross-strait ties, spurring diplomacy to end the U.S.-Iran war or erecting guardrails around artificial intelligence. China’s readout called on the U.S. to “adhere to the correct position of opposing ‘Taiwan independence’”, incorrectly but provocatively implying that the U.S. had changed its longstanding position (that it “does not support” that outcome). 18 September 2026 DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO Protesters streamed into the streets of Kinshasa Tuesday to decry the government’s proposals to change the constitution by popular referendum. One person was killed in clashes with police who intervened to stop the marchers from reaching parliament. Crisis Group expert Richard Moncrieff says the government’s main aim in trying to alter the constitution is to revise the clause imposing a two-term limit on presidents, thereby allowing the incumbent Félix Tshisekedi to stand for a third term. Tshisekedi is keen to hold the referendum soon, despite the opposition, because he senses that the country’s political balance has tilted in his favour. Going ahead with this vote may prove unwise, however, even if it comes off fairly smoothly. It may produce an illusion of political stability that, in turn, deflects attention from urgent tasks like reducing poverty among ordinary Congolese and taming the interlinked wars raging in the eastern provinces. MALI Algerian Prime Minister Sifi Ghrieb visited Bamako Monday in the latest sign of rapprochement between Algeria and Mali, whose relations had deteriorated badly in recent years. Crisis Group expert Jean-Hervé Jezequel says the thaw is welcome news for the Malian authorities. Bamako has been struggling to contain an insurgency linked to al-Qaeda, Jamaat Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), which killed 50 Malian soldiers in its latest attack on an army base last week. JNIM has lately allied with northern separatists who have also been fighting the Malian army. Historically, Algiers has been an important mediator between Bamako and northern armed groups. The warming of Algeria-Mali relations raises hopes that it might again play such a role, though maybe a more limited one given the Malian authorities’ increasingly sovereignist mindset. It could nevertheless help mitigate the conflict that has torn at Mali since 2012. PHILIPPINES Regional parliamentary elections took place on Monday in the Bangsamoro, the swathe of the southern Philippines that won autonomy in 2019 as part of a 2014 peace agreement between Manila and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF). At least five people were killed and twenty injured during the vote, though violence was less widespread than feared, with incidents concentrated in a few locations. No party secured an absolute majority, meaning that politicians will likely need to form a coalition. Crisis Group expert Georgi Engelbrecht says the incoming government, slated for inauguration by 30 October, will likely pair former MILF rebels with representatives of the region’s traditional political clans, unless the ex-insurgents, who have split into two factions, can reunite. The elections were a big step forward for the Bangsamoro peace process, with all eyes now on a crucial meeting between national government and MILF delegations to discuss gaps in fulfilling the 2014 accord’s terms. 11 September 2026 IRAN The International Atomic Energy Agency referred Iran to the UN Security Council Wednesday for breaching its nuclear non-proliferation obligations, marking the first time in twenty years the organisation has taken such a step. Tehran condemned the decision, blaming U.S. and Israeli strikes on its nuclear facilities for disrupting the agency’s inspections. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says concerns about Iran’s lacklustre cooperation with the UN watchdog have been mounting for years, capped by over a year of blocked access to key sites bombed by the U.S. and Israel in June 2025. Given that UN sanctions were already reinstated last year, and the expectation that China and Russia will shield it from additional punitive measures at the Security Council, the referral may harden Iran’s obduracy rather than cajole it into overdue cooperation. LEBANON Israel stepped up its attacks in southern Lebanon over the weekend with strikes that killed nearly 30 people and wounded dozens more. While Israel claimed that it had targeted Hizbollah arms caches and military installations, the assaults killed several children and medical staff. Crisis Group expert David Wood says Israel’s lethal escalation could continue, unless it faces strong pressure from the U.S., its most important ally, to desist. Washington sponsored a Lebanon-Israel ceasefire struck in late June but, over two months later, the deal remains largely unfulfilled, with Israeli military action continuing and Hizbollah refusing to disarm. SOMALIA Somali piracy has seen an uptick this year, with at least six hijackings of cargo ships and smaller vessels since April. The turmoil resulting from the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran has created opportune conditions for pirates, with fewer naval patrols off the Somali coast and more commercial traffic in nearby waters as ships are diverted from the Bab al-Mandab and the Strait of Hormuz. Crisis Group expert Omar Mahmood says the number of pirate attacks is far below what it was during the heyday of Red Sea piracy fifteen years ago. The current trajectory is concerning, however, and more raids are bound to occur, absent international and local measures both offshore and on land to combat the phenomenon. 4 September 2026 HAITI Armed gang members stormed the commune of Kenscoff, overlooking Port-au-Prince, overnight on 23-24 August, killing at least 47 people and abducting more than 50, whom they threatened to kill if security forces go after the gang in that area. At least thirteen abductees have subsequently been released. Briefing the UN Security Council on 28 August, UN envoy Carlos Ruiz Massieu said the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) would beef up its presence in the capital, while Haitian units would send reinforcements to Kenscoff. He also urged the GSF, which remains far short of its planned 5,500-person strength, to deploy in full without delay. Crisis Group expert Diego Da Rin says the Kenscoff massacre is the latest indication that gangs are on the offensive as the GSF assembles. U.S. - IRAN After a month-long lull, the U.S. resumed attacks on Iranian soil over the weekend, first striking rocket launchers on Larak island that Washington said were preparing to deploy sea mines, then hitting dozens of military targets along Iran’s southern coast. Tehran responded with missile and drone fire at bases hosting U.S. forces in the Gulf. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says the uptick comes as the Trump administration tries to isolate Tehran financially through increased sanctions and a naval blockade, while in parallel undermining Iranian efforts to control the Strait of Hormuz by escorting vessels through the waterway. While Washington's approach is to squeeze wherever possible and strike whenever it deems necessary – for example, in response to Iranian strikes or efforts to rebuild its military capabilities – the Islamic Republic could counter with additional strikes of its own on U.S. assets and allies, along with further attacks on shipping. THAILAND Overnight on 22 August, militants in Thailand’s three southernmost provinces staged over 50 attacks in four hours, including bombings and arson attempts at local administrative offices, shops and other buildings. Three passersby were injured. Further incidents followed on 23 and 29 August despite tightened security. Authorities blamed Barisan Revolusi Nasional Patani Melayu (Patani-Malay National Revolutionary Front, BRN), which has fought Bangkok’s rule since 2004. Such coordinated attacks are routine, says Crisis Group expert Matt Wheeler, but the scale of this campaign was unusual. It was likely intended to discredit the state, demonstrate insurgents’ reach and heighten pressure on the government to resume peace talks that have occurred intermittently since 2013. Thailand’s chief negotiator has reportedly proposed bringing technical-level talks with BRN forward from October to this month, in part to determine the reasons for the attacks. 21 August 2026 CHINA - SOUTH KOREA Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi paid a two-day visit to South Korea this week to discuss bilateral ties, Korean peninsula tensions and broader Asian affairs. The trip came three days after U.S. President Donald Trump ordered the Pentagon to scale back joint military exercises with South Korea. Trump also said he is willing to meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, as he did during his first term. These two unilateral announcements in turn prompted South Korean President Lee Jae-myung to reiterate his call for Seoul to bolster its own defences, for instance by acquiring nuclear-powered submarines and regaining independent control of its military in the event of hostilities. (Its forces would now be under U.S. command in a wartime contingency.) Crisis Group expert William Yang says the U.S.-South Korean friction has given Beijing an opening to deepen its own engagement with Seoul. It may now seek to present itself as the main mediator on the Korean peninsula, given its links with Pyongyang. ISRAEL - SYRIA Israeli warplanes bombed the Abu al-Duhur air base in northern Syria early Tuesday morning, in what Israel said was a warning against “deployment” of Turkish military personnel at the site. No casualties were reported. In remarks protesting the strike, Syrian Foreign Minister Assad al-Shaibani said Turkish officers had visited the base three days previously, but only for “training” purposes as Syrian forces refurbish the base. Tom Barrack, the U.S. ambassador to Türkiye who doubles as envoy for Syria, described Israel’s action as “unnecessary”. The backdrop, says Crisis Group expert Noah Bonsey, is an impasse in Israeli-Syrian talks about a bilateral security agreement. In these U.S.-mediated negotiations, under way since last summer, the Syrian government is seeking Israel’s withdrawal from parts of southern Syria it has occupied since December 2024, while Israel presses for limits on Turkish support for the Syrian military, among other security guarantees. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has pledged to retain a “buffer zone” in Syria as he campaigns for re-election in October. SOMALIA Local paramilitaries clashed with federal forces Monday in Baidoa, capital of Southwest state, leaving 30 dead, according to the Somali government. The militia is loyal to Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed “Lafta-Gareen”, a former state president whom Mogadishu forcibly removed in March after a disagreement over state elections. Lafta-Gareen fled to the Kenyan capital Nairobi, but his followers have been seeking to reinstate him, making regular incursions into Baidoa from a base on its northern outskirts. They reject the new state president who took office after a hastily organised vote following Lafta-Gareen’s ouster. Crisis Group expert Omar Mahmood says Monday’s attack was the largest and deadliest to date. Calm has since returned to Baidoa, but absent an initiative to address lingering grievances over the political transition in Southwest state, further violence is likely. 14 August 2026 IRAN - U.S. Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis attacked a merchant vessel Tuesday near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, killing six people aboard, as the U.S. fired two missiles at a cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman to enforce its renewed blockade of Iran-bound maritime traffic. The strikes came as both U.S. President Donald Trump and Iran claimed to have “total control” over the Strait of Hormuz. The Islamic Republic and Oman are in negotiations over a deal to partially reopen this crucial waterway. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says these consultations are part of a scramble by mediators to nudge the U.S. and Iran back into a truce, without which any bilateral understanding about the strait is unlikely to get much traction. SUDAN The paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and allied militias made rapid gains in Blue Nile state this week, taking Geissan town from the Sudanese army Tuesday and advancing into Kurmuk town Wednesday. The RSF appeared to use Ethiopian territory to launch the attacks on the two towns, both of which sit along the border with Ethiopia. Crisis Group expert Alan Boswell says the latest clashes will further drive up tensions between Sudan’s army and Addis Ababa, which accuse each other of supporting their domestic foes. Just two weeks earlier, clashes broke out between the Ethiopian military and opposing Tigray forces along a different part of the Sudan-Ethiopia border. WEST BANK Israeli settlers accompanied by soldiers besieged Palestinians in homes near the village of Qusra Sunday, among them Palestinians with U.S. citizenship. Only after four days and under U.S. pressure did the Israeli army intervene – not to chase away the settlers, but to remove a number of the Palestinians. It is another incident revealing the current Israeli government’s agenda for the West Bank, says Crisis Group expert Mairav Zonszein. The government is grabbing land, not only to create facts on the ground that will be hard for any successor to reverse, but to drive Palestinians into isolated, shrinking enclaves. 7 August 2026 CEUTA More than a hundred people died last week when Moroccan authorities apparently loosened controls along the border with Ceuta, a Spanish-administered enclave at the north-eastern tip of Morocco on the Strait of Gibraltar, unleashing an unprecedented rush of would-be emigrants into the territory. Most of those who perished were trying to swim or wade around coastal breakwaters. Following a swift Spanish military deployment, the vast majority of those who entered were returned or voluntarily went back to Morocco within days. Migrant testimony and video footage suggests that Moroccan security services helped facilitate the influx, says Crisis Group expert Riccardo Fabiani. They have previously used the spectre of unregulated migration to strong-arm Madrid into supporting Rabat’s claim to Western Sahara. Why they would use it this time is unclear. A few possible explanations come to mind: to impress upon Spain that its claim to Ceuta (which Morocco disputes) is hard to defend; to remind Madrid that it needs Rabat to protect its interests; and to earn credit with two allies, Israel and the U.S., with which the Spanish government has been at odds over Gaza and the war with Iran. CHAD The Chadian government filed a letter with the UN in late July declaring its intent to withdraw from the International Criminal Court (ICC). It is the fourth African country to take this step since 2025, after Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger. All have cited perceived anti-African bias, pointing to the fact that most of the ICC’s recent probes have focused on African countries. The Trump administration, which has sanctioned the ICC for its investigation of Israeli actions in Gaza, called on more African nations to “reclaim their sovereignty” by following in Chad’s footsteps. Crisis Group expert Enrica Picco says some Chadians will welcome N’djamena’s move on these grounds. Many, however, will see it as a way to curry favour with Washington to secure its help in counter-terrorism efforts around Lake Chad. Still others – especially among the Zaghawa ethnic group – may espy a government attempt to escape international scrutiny for complicity in crimes in neighbouring Sudan. N’djamena is accused of allowing the United Arab Emirates to funnel arms to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, who have massacred Zaghawa and others in Darfur. ETHIOPIA Hundreds of people have fled into Sudan after clashes last weekend in Shererina, a western district of Ethiopia’s northernmost Tigray province. The fighting flared up along the Ethiopia-Sudan border between the Ethiopian army and forces loyal to the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). It quickly subsided, but not before raising fears of renewed open hostilities between these two sides, which fought a bloody war from 2020 to 2022. Tensions between the TPLF and Addis Ababa have been rising for months, especially after it ousted an interim regional administration established under a 2022 peace deal and reinstalled its own chair as regional president in April. The two sides now accuse each other of soliciting help from one of the main belligerents in Sudan. Independent details of the clashes are scarce, says Crisis Group expert Alan Boswell, but clearly neither side wanted to escalate further at this time. Nevertheless, the border confrontation shows how dangerous the standoff has become. 24 July 2026 THAILAND Militants attacked a checkpoint in Narathiwat, a province on the Malaysian border, on Wednesday, killing four paramilitaries, known as rangers, and an army senior non-commissioned officer. Six assailants in the bed of a pickup truck fired assault rifles and threw pipe bombs, stealing the rangers’ weapons and body armour before fleeing. They also wounded six civilians, including three children, one seriously. The army’s chief of staff, General Chaiyapruek Duangpraphat, used unusually strong language afterward, saying, “I will have my men hunt [the perpetrators] down in every village and forested mountain area. Let those who provide shelter and the countries that harbour them know this”. Crisis Group expert Matt Wheeler says attacks are routine in the country’s deep south, which has been troubled by an insurgency since 2004. These incidents rarely grab national attention, but this one is distinctive for the high death toll and the popular anger excited by widely viewed video footage of what happened. U.S. - IRAN The U.S. and Iran continued to trade blows this week, putting Washington’s Middle Eastern allies in the crosshairs of Iranian drone and missile launch teams while U.S. forces enforced a renewed naval blockade of Iran and conducted daily strikes on sites inside the country. On Wednesday, President Donald Trump pledged to “destroy one bridge or power plant” every time Tehran fires at a vessel transiting the Strait of Hormuz – a threat quickly met by warnings of retaliation in kind by the Islamic Republic. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says both sides appear convinced that inflicting greater physical damage and economic pain plays to their strengths, even at the risk of significant escalation. For now, this dynamic is persisting despite efforts by mediators to dial down tensions. YEMEN The Houthi rebels declared a “maritime embargo” on Saudi Arabia Monday, vowing to strike any Saudi-linked vessel passing from the Red Sea through Bab al-Mandab, the strait connecting those waters to the Gulf of Oman. A de facto truce had held between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen’s internationally recognised government from 2022 until last week, when Saudi warplanes bombed the Sanaa airport and the Houthis fired missiles at the kingdom in respo nse. On Wednesday, Saudi officials said an oil tanker caught fire after the Houthis struck it near the kingdom’s Red Sea port of Jizan. The foreign ministry in Riyadh said Saudi Arabia would take all necessary measures to defend itself, while U.S. President Donald Trump said the U.S. would inflict “major military punishment” upon both the Houthis and their ally Iran if they attack shipping again. Crisis Group expert Ahmed Nagi says the risk of open hostilities, both in the Red Sea and along front lines in Yemen, is rising dramatically. 17 July 2026 CUBA Cuba’s power grid collapsed Tuesday for the third time in less than ten days and the sixth time so far in 2026. The island’s severe energy shortages began in January when the U.S. imposed an oil blockade, triggering a humanitarian crisis. The blockade is part of the Trump administration’s pressure campaign to bring about wholesale political and economic change in Cuba, as negotiations between the two countries stall. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says the U.S. appears to be using civilian pain as a weapon in its effort to oust Cuba’s communist regime. Havana should pursue meaningful and much needed reforms, regardless of what the U.S. does. But in the meantime Washington should lift the blockade so as not to create a humanitarian crisis in the pursuit of its goals, and avoid any further escalation. The AAKG was initially aligned with Bangui but later broke with the government after its rapprochement with a Fulani-led armed group that the militia accuses of encroaching on Zandé land. Crisis Group expert Fulbert Ngodji says the AAKG may be digging in to battle the state. Stability during Touadéra’s new term will hinge on promoting intercommunal dialogue in the south east, better integrating militias under army command, and reducing regional isolation through development and security reform. IRAN The falling value of Iran's national currency sparked demonstrations that since late December have grown into nationwide anti-regime unrest. The government has altered its subsidy policies but done little to dampen wider grievances. At least three dozen people have been killed as state forces crack down on protests that show little sign of slowing down. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says the Islamic Republic faces a major dilemma: it is neither willing nor able to adopt reforms that could meet expectations for political, social and economic change and on notice from U.S. President Donald Trump that outside intervention is possible if its repression intensifies. LEBANON Lebanon said it had passed a milestone in disarming Hizbollah, but the country’s fragile ceasefire deal with Israel remains imperilled. On Thursday, the Lebanese army announced that it had brought all weapons under state control in the southern area between the Litani River and the Israeli border. Israel immediately disputed the army’s assertion, saying Hizbollah retains military infrastructure in that region. Crisis Group expert David Wood says Beirut faces dangers ahead in any case. The army must soon move toward disarming Hizbollah north of the Litani, where the group refuses to comply – driving up the risk of internal discord. Yet Lebanese leaders also know that Israel will almost certainly respond to any hold-ups in disarming Hizbollah with severe military escalations, inflicting still more pain on their embattled country. How Algeria’s Rupture with the UAE Could Roil the Region mloukili Fri, 10/23/2026 - 10:58 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Algeria's President Abdelmadjid Tebboune (L) speaks with United Arab Emirates’ President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan as they pose for a photo during the G7 Summit hosted by Italy, in Savelletri, on 14 June, 2024. AFP / Ludovic Marin Commentary / Middle East & North Africa 23 October 2026 13 minutes How Algeria’s Rupture with the UAE Could Roil the Region Algiers has severed diplomatic ties with Abu Dhabi, following years of discord over crises in North Africa and the Sahel. The two countries see their dispute very differently, but it has nonetheless become a rivalry that could put regional stability at risk. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Also available in Arabic English Arabic Michaël Béchir Ayari Senior Analyst, Tunisia Related Tags Algeria United Arab Emirates On 10 September, Algeria broke off diplomatic relations with the United Arab Emirates, in the latest manifestation of a confrontation between the two countries over policy in the Middle East, North Africa and the Sahel. Since 2020, disagreements have festered between Algiers and Abu Dhabi over Israel, Morocco and Western Sahara. Algeria has also grown increasingly suspicious of the aims of Emirati involvement in crises in Libya, Sudan and Sahelian states. The rupture is marked by an asymmetry of perceptions. Algiers sees the UAE, sitting far away in the Gulf, as interfering in its North African and Sahelian neighbourhood, where it is looking to rebuild the diplomatic clout that it wielded for decades after winning independence from French colonial rule in 1962. It views Emirati interventions as, at the very least, encroachments upon its historical domain. Abu Dhabi, for its part, says economic ties, not Algeria, are central to its African engagement. It forswears any intent to provoke or sideline Algiers. The bilateral discord has become a full-blown rivalry, however, and one that is becoming perilous as regional security arrangements are changing. Algeria is forging closer links with Niger, as well as with Chad. It is also backing the Sudanese army in its war with the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and Libya’s internationally recognised government in Tripoli in its power struggle with Field Marshal Khalifa Haftar, whose forces control the country’s east . Algerian officials describe these moves as reinforcing the country’s “ strategic borders ”. Algeria remains bitterly at odds with Morocco over Western Sahara and other issues, and it is just now repairing relations with Mali. Meanwhile, the UAE is forming its own partnerships in North Africa and the Sahel, which can involve both states and armed groups, and which often (though not always) put it indirectly in competition with Algeria. A direct clash between the two countries is unlikely. Their respective alliance systems overlap somewhat and do not constitute coherent groups of adversaries. Still, jostling among them could draw in Algeria, the UAE or both, with the risk of local escalation or inadvertent confrontation. Roots of the Break-up Dramatic as the 10 September rupture was, it had been a long time coming. Until 2020, relations between Algeria and the UAE were strong. In the early 1970s, Algeria sent oil experts, including executives from Sonatrach, Algeria’s state-owned hydrocarbons company, to the Gulf to help establish the institutions that would become the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company. Abdelaziz Bouteflika, who served as Algeria’s president between 1999 and 2019, lived in Abu Dhabi from 1984 to 1987, working as a diplomatic adviser to Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan, father of today’s leader Mohammed bin Zayed (aka MBZ). During Bouteflika’s tenure as Algerian head of state, Emirati capital made significant inroads into the Algerian economy, including in the defence sector. In 2012, for example, Emirati investors cooperated with the Algerian defence ministry and state-owned companies in joint ventures to produce Mercedes-Benz vehicles and Emirati-designed NIMR armoured vehicles in Algeria. The UAE built networks of contacts within the Algerian political, business and military elite, some of which survived Bouteflika’s fall in 2019. The UAE’s 2020 normalisation with Israel – part of what is known as the Abraham Accords – opened a first crack in the relationship. Algiers firmly opposed any Arab state forging ties with Israel before a comprehensive settlement of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. In September 2020, President Abdelmadjid Tebboune criticised what he described as a “ rush ” ( empressement ) toward normalisation, declaring that Algeria would not be part of it. Algiers has long been the foremost outside backer of the Polisario Front, the group battling for an independent Western Sahara. Algerian concerns grew further when, on 4 November 2020, the UAE became the first Arab country to open a consulate in Western Sahara, establishing a diplomatic office in Laayoune, a city in the Moroccan-controlled part of the disputed territory. Algiers has long been the foremost outside backer of the Polisario Front, the group battling for an independent Western Sahara. Sabri Boukadoum, then Algeria’s foreign minister, questioned the move’s compatibility with international law and reaffirmed Algerian support for Sahrawi self-determination. A month later, Morocco followed the UAE in normalising relations with Israel, prompting Algerian authorities to discern an emerging UAE-Morocco-Israel alliance in their immediate vicinity. This perception was significantly reinforced in November 2021, when Morocco and Israel signed a landmark defence cooperation agreement . The agreement formalised defence ties and paved the way for cooperation in areas including intelligence and military training. Algerian authorities viewed this deepening partnership as tantamount to a direct threat , part of a regional alignment aimed at weakening their country. Algerian worries extended to allegations of foreign interference in domestic affairs. Officials accused Morocco and Israel of supporting the Movement for the Self-Determination of Kabylia (MAK) , an independence movement that Algeria designated a terrorist organisation in 2021. As evidence, they pointed to the fact that Morocco’s representative at the UN had publicly argued that the Kabyle people are entitled to exercise a right to self-determination . A number of former Algerian diplomats and commentators implicated the UAE in these purported destabilisation efforts as well: a Morocco-based think-tank separately reported on contacts between MAK representatives and Emirati figures, citing sources within the Kabyle independence movement, among others. The Dispute Deepens Other regional disagreements added to the tensions. In 2020 and again in 2022 , Abu Dhabi opposed the appointment of successive Algerian foreign ministers as UN envoys to Libya, against the backdrop of Emirati support for Field Marshal Haftar, and Algeria’s closer links with the authorities in Tripoli. The UAE cited the objections of Arab states and Libyan actors, expressing their concern that Algeria, as a neighbouring country deeply involved in the conflict, could not be viewed as an impartial mediator. Another friction point surfaced in 2023, when Algerian government-aligned media attributed the failure of Algeria’s BRICS application to Emirati manoeuvring against its candidacy. Views in Algiers on how to counter the UAE’s gambits – real and perceived – may not have been entirely aligned. Some elements of the security establishment and associated media favoured a confrontational approach, while others, including figures close to former army Chief of Staff Ahmed Gaïd Salah, worried about jeopardising significant economic interests and longstanding personal connections. The exact boundaries of these contrasting viewpoints, however, remained unclear. As Emirati actions increasingly clashed with Algeria’s regional priorities and came to be perceived as national security threats , displaying restraint became more difficult. Despite his initial reticence to comment on the matter, President Tebboune’s criticism of the UAE gradually became louder. Despite his initial reticence to comment on the matter, President Tebboune’s criticism of the UAE gradually became louder. In 2024, he complained that wherever conflict erupted in the region , the money of an unnamed Gulf state could be found behind it; in 2025, he said Algeria enjoyed good relations with all Gulf monarchies, except one . By the following February, he was openly denouncing a “ mini-state ” that was destabilising the Arab world and the Sahel. Successive attempts to ease tensions made little headway. Former Algerian diplomats told Crisis Group that Gulf states, including Bahrain and Oman, sent emissaries to Algiers to try mediating between the two sides. They said Algeria rejected these efforts, however, and will keep doing so as long as what it regards as Emirati meddling continues. Direct contacts endured, but they failed to achieve a thaw. By February, when Algeria terminated the 2013 bilateral agreement that provided the legal framework for air travel between the two countries, the room for compromise had considerably narrowed. Rivalry in the Sahel As relations deteriorated, the dispute increasingly spilled into a contest for influence in North Africa and the Sahel. A May 2024 tour of Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso by UAE Minister of State Sheikh Shakhboot bin Nahyan Al Nahyan raised hackles in Algeria , which has long described Mali in particular as a “brother” nation. Abu Dhabi was offering the Sahelian capitals cooperation on counter-terrorism just as Western influence was waning in the region and the new Alliance of Sahel States (AES) was opening it to new external patrons. There were other angles as well: for the UAE, security cooperation is inseparable from economic interests, particularly when it comes to natural resources; Dubai’s role in the international gold trade, including gold originating in the Sahel, gave the UAE an additional stake in regional developments. Meanwhile, Algeria’s historical ties with Bamako and the other AES capitals were reaching a nadir. Emirati officials maintain that its engagement was not aimed at supplanting Algeria. Indeed, they rarely present Algiers as a competitor when discussing the Sahel or any other African region. Rather, they say, Abu Dhabi is pursuing a broad strategy, rooted in geo-economics , designed to expand the UAE’s footprint on a continent that has gained in importance. As an Emirati businessman and former government official told Crisis Group in explaining the scope of Abu Dhabi’s ambition, “You’re either at the table or on the menu”. Algerian officials, by contrast, view the UAE’s combination of investments and partnerships with governments, business elites and armed actors as a means of undermining their country’s interests. They regard the Sahel as crucial to Algerian security, particularly since Bamako abandoned the Algeria-mediated 2015 peace agreement with armed separatists in northern Mali, whom they fear could make common cause with co-ethnics on the Algerian side of the border. Algerian concerns were heightened by allegations of ransom payments , mentioned in an August UN report and linked to the UAE by regional sources , to the jihadist group JNIM that has grabbed chunks of Malian and other Sahelian state territory. Algiers has long argued that such payments strengthen armed groups active near its frontiers. The contrast in approach and threat perceptions became particularly acute over events in Niger. Following a 2023 coup there, relations between Algiers and Niamey soured, and they worsened further in April 2025, when Niger recalled its ambassador from Algiers in solidarity with authorities in Bamako, with whom Algiers was then at loggerheads over the abrogated peace agreement and other issues. Bilateral ties subsequently improved, following Nigerien leader General Abdourahamane Tiani’s visit to Algiers the following February . The two countries revived their security cooperation, and Niger even helped broker the present rapprochement between Algeria and Mali. Relations with Niger ... have an important economic dimension for both Algeria and the UAE. Relations with Niger also have an important economic dimension for both Algeria and the UAE. Algeria considers Niger key to its effort to reconnect with sub-Saharan Africa through energy and trade. Its flagship project is the Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline , intended to carry Nigerian gas through Niger into Algeria and onward to Europe. Here, the UAE has a competing interest: the Trans-Saharan route directly competes with Morocco’s Atlantic pipeline , which is expected to run along the West African coast and which the UAE has backed with early financing. It is against this backdrop that Algeria viewed a failed coup against Tiani on 29 August as threatening its interests. Rumours swirled in Algiers about an Emirati hand . To date, these are unsubstantiated, but they have only deepened suspicions regarding the UAE’s activities in the Sahel. Algeria responded to the coup attempt by deploying four Su-30MKA fighter jets to Niamey , accompanied by an Il-78 aerial-refuelling aircraft and an Il-76 transport plane. Algerian analysts told Crisis Group that mechanics, logistics specialists and personnel for force protection were also dispatched. Beyond sending a clear signal of support for Tiani’s government, these steps showcased Algeria’s determination to regain influence in a region where it has lost considerable ground – and where it appears to have identified the UAE as a chief antagonist. Algeria’s actions also embodied something more, again with implications for relations with the UAE: a shift away from its longstanding aversion to military operations abroad. Since independence, Algeria’s leaders have framed the country’s foreign policy around non-alignment, anti-imperialism, national sovereignty, diplomatic mediation, South-South solidarity, support for national liberation and self-determination movements, and, importantly, non-interference in other states’ domestic affairs. There have been exceptions, and Algeria has at times interpreted this last precept flexibly when it has felt that it has important interests at stake. Overall, however, reluctance to dispatch regular military forces abroad has remained a powerful institutional constraint. Only in 2020 did a constitutional amendment create a legal framework for overseas deployments. The latter still require parliamentary approval and are restricted to internationally sanctioned missions. More recently, the army’s top general Saïd Chengriha has promoted the concept that Algeria has “ strategic borders ”. Though it does not formally establish a right to military intervention in neighbouring countries, this notion expands Algeria’s security perimeter by treating instability, armed groups and trafficking networks beyond its frontiers as potential national security threats. Rivalry in North Africa and the Horn In other regional conflicts, Algeria and the UAE likewise stand on opposing sides. In Libya, Field Marshal Haftar’s forces have, over time, received extensive Emirati backing . In contrast, Algeria has stood with Tripoli (which itself has maintained tight relations with Niger). In Sudan, Algeria sides with the army, whose leaders it considers the country’s legitimate representatives; several Algerian analysts told Crisis Group that in 2025 Algiers discreetly provided the Sudanese army with equipment, including old Russian MiG-29 fighter jets and spare parts. By contrast, Abu Dhabi refers to the army-led administration as the “ Port Sudan authority ”, in reference to its erstwhile seat in Port Sudan, treating it merely as one party to the conflict; it is widely believed to be sending support to the army’s main adversary, the RSF, though the UAE denies the claim. The divergent policies toward Sudan have had wider repercussions. Eastern and southern Libya reportedly have served as logistical corridors for supplies to the RSF allegedly originating with the Emirates . Previously, much of this materiel allegedly went through eastern Chad. For its part, the UAE maintains that its activities in eastern Chad are humanitarian , particularly getting aid to Sudanese refugees. An Algerian expert told Crisis Group that policymakers in Algiers appear intent on deepening ties with N’Djamena at least in part to counterbalance what they view as Sudan-linked Emirati networks in Chad. That said, Chadian President Idriss Déby has invested considerable political capital in his relationship with the UAE, whose substantial financial support , including a $1.5 billion budget financing agreement signed in 2023, gives the latter sway that Algeria would struggle to match. The growing Algeria-UAE rivalry could deepen existing Libyan divisions and turn local disputes into arenas of indirect regional confrontation. These competing relationships run the risk of reinforcing regional divisions, with Field Marshal Haftar and Chad being generally close to Abu Dhabi, while Tripoli and Niger cooperate more with Algiers. Conversely, the growing Algeria-UAE rivalry could deepen existing Libyan divisions and turn local disputes into arenas of indirect regional confrontation. To some extent, it already has. In August 2024, for example, Haftar’s forces moved toward Ghadames, only a few kilometres from the Algerian frontier, a development Algiers saw as threatening. The crisis eventually subsided after Haftar’s spokesman denied that the city was a military objective and insisted that the border with Algeria was secure . Still, the episode reinforced perceptions in Algiers of a UAE-backed menace in its neighbourhood. Tensions continue to build. Algeria is increasingly concerned by Haftar’s influence in southern Libya, where his forces have tightened their grip on lucrative trafficking routes and strengthened cooperation with N’Djamena in fighting Chadian rebel groups. Haftar has thus obtained access to an important source of income and displaced Chadian rebels toward northern Niger, particularly the strategic Salvador Pass area , exacerbating instability near Algeria’s southern border. All in all, these developments help explain Algeria’s evolving approach to regional security. Rather than viewing events in Libya, Niger and Sudan separately, Algiers increasingly sees them as interconnected challenges. Containing the Clash What began as a downturn in Algerian-UAE relations has thus evolved into a full-blown crisis with possible reverberations across the northern third of Africa. Algeria has remained silent as to why precisely it severed diplomatic ties. The foreign ministry’s statement was vague , referring to “provocative or hostile” actions as well as warnings that had failed to deter Abu Dhabi from unspecified behaviour. Algeria may have avoided identifying grievances or conditions for reconciliation in order to allow for flexibility in future talks. The difficulty of substantiating its complaints may also have contributed to its ambiguous stance. To officials in Abu Dhabi, the break was both unanticipated and perplexing. Though he did not name Algeria, Anwar Gargash, a diplomatic adviser to the UAE president, alluded to it in a tweet complaining of “ puzzles and signals that require decoding ” in interstate relations. The UAE foreign ministry adopted a more conciliatory tone, expressing hope that the rupture would prove temporary. A number of Emirati analysts said the dispute is of far greater significance to Algeria than to the UAE, given Abu Dhabi’s preoccupation with the war in the Gulf. These reactions underscore a divergence in perspectives: while Algiers views Abu Dhabi’s alliances as a growing threat to its regional influence, Abu Dhabi sees its engagement as part of a strategy driven by political, economic and security interests that go beyond any bilateral relationship. In reality, neither country can bar the other from an ever more cutthroat arena. Too, governments and armed groups in the region cannot be neatly categorised into two rival blocs; each of Niger, Chad and the assorted Libyan players has its own agenda that may not align precisely with either Algerian or Emirati wishes. Still, as Algeria assumes a more assertive stance and the UAE pursues its geographically expansive approach, seemingly oblivious to, or at least underestimating the depth of Algeria’s concerns and its conviction that Abu Dhabi is challenging its position, bilateral tensions risk becoming more fraught. Informal communication channels could help shed light on their respective intentions and minimise the chance of misinterpretation and accidental conflict. The two countries would be far better served by taking steps and shifting their mindsets to help ensure that Emirati influence in Algeria’s neighbourhood, and Algiers’ response to it, do not become a trigger for bilateral confrontation. First, though full reconciliation may be out of reach for the moment, maintaining or restoring informal communication channels could help shed light on their respective intentions and minimise the chance of misinterpretation and accidental conflict. Secondly, Algiers should avoid construing every Emirati undertaking in neighbouring countries as part of a strategy directed against its interests. Finally, Abu Dhabi ought to take Algeria’s security concerns more seriously. It should recognise that its regional partnerships, particularly those involving armed non-state actors, may threaten Algerian interests, even when not so intended. Both countries should have an interest in preventing local disputes from drawing them further toward confrontation, particularly given that both neighbouring governments and armed groups pursue agendas neither side can fully control. Absent such efforts, the rift could deepen, increasing the risk that local crises spiral into open hostility. The result would be to exacerbate tensions in a region already riven by deadly conflict. Brazil: New Evidence of Serious Police Misconduct in Deadly Raid. Play Video Read a text description of this video TEXT ON SCREEN October 28, 2025 Rio de Janeiro, Brazil NARRATION On the morning of October 28th, 2025, hundreds of police officers surrounded two low-income neighborhoods in Rio de Janeiro. By nightfall, the operation would become the deadliest in Brazil's history. TEXT ON SCREEN WARNING. This video contains graphic content, including blurred images of dead bodies. Viewer discretion advised. NARRATION 122 people were killed, including two children and five police officers. According to the autopsy records, over eighty five percent of non-police victims were Black. Police in Rio de Janeiro are required by Supreme Court order to wear body cameras. However, only twenty-three percent of officers wore body cameras that day, and in the footage reviewed by Human Rights Watch, not a single killing was captured on camera. LOWER THIRD Damir Khairat Research Technologist Digital Investigations Lab NARRATION Human Rights Watch was given access to the prosecutor's investigation into the operation, including 8,800 pages of records, 122 autopsies, and nearly 4,000 hours of body camera footage. TEXT ON SCREEN Prosecutors have released the body camera footage shown in this video. Most footage is sealed as evidence and cannot be published. NARRATION Watching all the footage day and night without any breaks would have taken a single researcher almost six months. So, we trained several artificial intelligence models to help us identify the moments that mattered most. First, we needed to organize everything. The models, alongside software that Human Rights Watch developed, synchronized recordings from different officers, mapped their locations, and scanned footage for gunshots and signs of camera tampering. From there we had a searchable platform that let us view the operation as one coordinated event, rather than thousands of separate recordings. What we found was evidence of widespread tampering and obstruction of body cameras. And it consistently happened at the exact moment cameras should have been recording, during arrests, shootouts, or while officers entered homes. Authorities said that the purpose of the raid was to arrest suspected drug traffickers. The evidence we found points to an operation that appeared lethal by design. To explain how we came to this conclusion, let's look at some examples of the moments we trained our AI models to detect. An officer's camera captured this video in an alleyway as a large group of his colleagues pass by, after which the officer quickly covers his camera. He or another officer then flags that there's a camera recording. SOUNDBITE [IN PORTUGUESE] The team has a camera. The team has a camera. No, no I’m talking about the thing there. NARRATION It's unclear why he covered it, but prosecutors later charged him with camera tampering. SOUNDBITE So, this would be the kind of like overall operational view. NARRATION To find incidents like this across almost 4,000 hours of footage from nearly 500 officers, we trained a model to detect similar moments when a camera continued recording, but the lens was covered. Here, an officer is seen struggling to pick the lock on the door of someone's home. Once it's open, he removes his camera and leaves it unattended for over an hour, presumably while he's inside the home. Because the camera was still capturing an image, this recording wasn't initially flagged by our software. So, we trained a second model to identify "stale scenes" where the recording stays the same for long periods of time. As our models learned and improved, they uncovered lots of suspicious recording gaps. In the end, we documented more than 250 camera obstructions. Moments like these are exactly the situations that body cameras are meant to document, helping ensure that any unlawful behavior is captured and that circumstances surrounding the 122 killings can be properly investigated. Another method we used was an AI system that analyzes audio to detect gunshots. After we trained it specifically for Rio police body cameras and local conditions, the model successfully detected most gunshots in a test set of videos. We were also able to use AI to pull text directly from the videos, like the date, time, location and ID number of the officer wearing the camera. But one of the most striking findings came from what we didn't see. Despite the scale of the operation and the number of deaths, we found no footage showing the killings themselves. NARRATION To understand what was missing, we organized body camera recordings across the operation using extracted timestamps. TEXT ON SCREEN Unusable footage Usable footage NARRATION We found that more than half the officers’ recordings had either ended or had significant gaps by noon. From there, the usable footage continued to decline, just as the operation became most deadly. The missing footage, combined with extensive evidence of camera tampering, suggests that body cameras were deliberately misused to prevent killings from being recorded. Throughout our investigation, AI was one tool out of many. Our team of researchers interviewed witnesses in Rio, visited the neighborhood where the killings took place, analyzed police records and autopsies, verified photographs and videos, and manually reviewed AI findings. What AI provided was speed and scale. It helped us process thousands of hours of footage, connect pieces of evidence, and focus our attention where it mattered most. In other words, AI helped us find needles in a very large haystack. Now, it's up to Brazilian prosecutors to thoroughly investigate both the killings and the decisions that led to such a deadly operation. Those who use disproportionate force or misuse body cameras should be held accountable. To learn more about the events of October 28th and Human Rights Watch’s findings, visit HRW.org and read our investigation, A Strategy of Death. Police officers tampered with body cameras and were responsible for serious investigative failures during an operation ostensibly to arrest gang members in a low-income neighborhood in Rio de Janeiro on October 28, 2025. A year-long Human Rights Watch investigation concluded that police breached Supreme Court orders and their own protocols during Operation Containment, which appeared to be lethal by design. Federal and state prosecutors should initiate criminal and civil proceedings to investigate those responsible for abuses, including senior officials and police commanders. (Rio de Janeiro, October 28, 2026) – Police officers tampered with body cameras and failed to take crucial investigative steps during an operation in a low-income neighborhood in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, on October 28, 2025, Human Rights Watch said in an investigation published today. Evidence indicates police used excessive force and may have intentionally killed scores of men and boys. The investigation, “‘A Strategy of Death’: Investigating Brazil’s Deadliest Police Operation,” documents Operation Containment (Operação Contenção), in which a total of 122 people were killed. This included two children and four police officers killed that day, and a fifth police officer who later succumbed to his wounds. An additional two men were killed in the early morning before the official start of the operation. Eighty-five percent of non-police victims of the October 2025 raid were Black. “A Strategy of Death” Investigating Brazil’s Deadliest Police Operation Read the full investigation here None of the killings were captured in the thousands of hours of body camera footage sent by Rio de Janeiro Military Police to the Public Defender’s Office, which Human Rights Watch reviewed after being granted access. “Human Rights Watch processed thousands of hours of body camera footage and analyzed videos, official investigation files, and autopsy records for every victim, yet crucial questions remain because police failed to properly record killings, preserve crime scenes, or collect crucial data,” said Sophia Jones, open source researcher with the Digital Investigations Lab at Human Rights Watch. “The families of those killed, including police officers, deserve answers and accountability with a thorough, independent investigation.” Human Rights Watch interviewed 41 witnesses, family members, and experts, and analyzed 4,400 hours of body camera footage, 9,000 pages of official investigation files, 122 autopsy reports, court records, and hundreds of videos and photographs. Human Rights Watch analyzed the data using several machine learning models built in-house, followed by manual review and assessment by researchers. Based on Human Rights Watch analysis of data from Rio-based security research lab GENI (Grupo de Estudos dos Novos Ilegalismos or Group for the Study of New Illegalities), nongovernmental think tank Fórum Brasileiro de Segurança Pública (Brazilian Public Security Forum), independent security monitoring organization Fogo Cruzado (Crossfire), and media reports, Operation Containment was the deadliest documented one-day police operation in a country where police forces kill more than 6,000 people per year. Human Rights Watch visited the Complexo da Penha, the site of the operation, six months after the raid and found that the criminal group Red Command (Comando Vermelho)—the target of the operation—continued to impose its rule on residents. Despite the stated goal of carrying out 100 arrest warrants for alleged Red Command members, police records show they arrested only 17 of those for whom they had warrants, although it is not clear whether those are the warrants that justified the operation or other pending warrants. Police did not enter the home of the local Red Command leader, for whom they had a warrant, a Civil Police commander told prosecutors, even though body camera footage shows police moving around it. Despite a state law and a Supreme Court order mandating that police wear body cameras, only about 23 percent of the 2,500 civil and military police officers who participated in the raid did, the Rio de Janeiro government said. Machine-Enabled Forensics How Human Rights Watch used Artificial Intelligence to Analyze Body Camera Footage from Rio’s Deadliest Police Raid Read the methodology here Human Rights Watch analysis of the footage of the 527 military police officers who wore the cameras found widespread tampering and obstruction of their use. Officers left cameras running before the operation, effectively draining batteries; covered lenses; placed cameras where they would not capture officers’ actions; and left cameras in vehicles. Such tampering consistently occurred at key moments, during arrests, shootouts, or while officers entered homes, researchers found. Most tampering was on cameras worn by officers whose units engaged in frontline operations, such as the Battalion of Special Police Operations of the Military Police, the unit deployed to the forested area where the majority of killings took place. Researchers determined that 36 percent of gunshot clusters heard on their cameras occurred when the cameras were obstructed. Body camera footage showed officers assaulting and threatening to kill detainees, including a child, whom they forced to lie down next to a dead body while photographing him. In another recording, an officer tells officers to shoot detainees in the legs if they ran. In a third clip, an officer expressed frustration that body cameras prevented them from killing suspects. Researchers also analyzed or verified hundreds of videos and photographs taken by members of the local community that day. In one series of verified videos, officers pile dead bodies, some with their genitalia exposed, into an armored police vehicle, while joking. “Look how wonderful,” one officer said. “We like this.” While police said they spent months planning the operation, there was no evidence that they made any advance preparations to protect crime scenes and conduct forensic analysis.
